cards.q: What does the abbreviation ECSC stand for? When was it founded, and which states were its founding members? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The European Coal and Steel Community, founded by the Treaty of Paris (signed 18 April 1951, in force 23 July 1952) by Belgium, France, (West) Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
• Background: Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950 – pooling coal and steel (the war industries) under a supranational High Authority, so that war between France and Germany became materially impossible (the EU as a peace project).
• Founders ('the Six'): BE, FR, DE, IT, LU, NL – the same six later signed the Treaties of Rome (EEC, Euratom, 1957).
• Duration: concluded for 50 years, the ECSC Treaty expired on 23 July 2002; coal and steel then fell under the general EC (now TFEU) rules.
Codex: not in the codex (historical) – know dates: 1950 Schuman · 1951/52 Paris · 1957/58 Rome · 2002 expiry.

cards.q: Assign each of the following innovations to the correct treaty and give the year it entered into force: (1) Union citizenship, Economic and Monetary Union and the 'three pillars'; (2) incorporation of the Schengen acquis and the sanction procedure for breaches of the Union's values; (3) institutional reform preparing the 2004 enlargement and the preventive 'clear risk' mechanism; (4) a legally binding Charter of Fundamental Rights, legal personality of the Union and a withdrawal clause. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) Maastricht 1993, (2) Amsterdam 1999, (3) Nice 2003, (4) Lisbon 2009.
• (1) Treaty of Maastricht (Treaty on European Union), signed 7 Feb 1992, in force 1 Nov 1993: founded the EU on three pillars (EC, CFSP, JHA), renamed the EEC 'EC', introduced Union citizenship, EMU (road to the euro), co-decision and the subsidiarity principle.
• (2) Treaty of Amsterdam, signed 1997, in force 1 May 1999: Schengen integrated into EU law, area of freedom, security and justice, sanction mechanism for serious and persistent breaches of the values (today Art 7(2)–(3) TEU), renumbering of the Treaties.
• (3) Treaty of Nice, signed 2001, in force 1 Feb 2003: reweighting of votes and Commission size for enlargement, preventive mechanism (today Art 7(1) TEU); the Charter was only solemnly proclaimed (not binding) at Nice in Dec 2000.
• (4) Treaty of Lisbon, signed 13 Dec 2007, in force 1 Dec 2009 (after the failed Constitutional Treaty, 2005 referenda in FR/NL): pillars abolished, EU replaces and succeeds the EC (Art 1(3) TEU), legal personality (Art 47 TEU), Charter binding (Art 6(1) TEU), European Council becomes an institution with a permanent President, OLP as default, Art 50 TEU.
• Earlier milestone for context: Single European Act (1986/87) – internal market by end-1992, more QMV.
Codex: Art 1(3), 6(1), 7, 47, 50 TEU – dates are not in the codex, learn them.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statements? Give reasons. (a) 'The European Union was founded by the Treaty of Lisbon.' (b) 'The European Coal and Steel Community still exists alongside the EU.' (c) 'Since the Treaty of Lisbon, both the European Community and Euratom have been absorbed into the European Union.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false.
• (a) False. The EU was founded by the Treaty of Maastricht (in force 1 Nov 1993). Lisbon (2009) reformed it: it abolished the pillar structure, merged the EC into the EU ('The Union shall replace and succeed the European Community', Art 1(3) TEU) and gave the Union legal personality (Art 47 TEU).
• (b) False. The ECSC Treaty (Paris 1951) was concluded for 50 years and expired on 23 July 2002; its assets and the coal and steel sector passed to the EC.
• (c) Partly false. The EC was absorbed (Art 1(3) TEU), but the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom, Rome 1957) continues to exist as a separate organisation under its own Treaty, which was only amended by a protocol annexed to the Treaty of Lisbon; it shares the EU institutions.
Codex: Art 1(3) TEU, Art 47 TEU (Euratom Treaty is a separate treaty).

cards.q: Valdaria, an EU Member State not yet using the euro, wants to adopt it. Its data: inflation 1.1 percentage points above the average of the three best-performing Member States in price stability; general government deficit 3.4% of GDP, and the Council has decided under Art 126(6) TFEU that an excessive deficit exists; public debt 55% of GDP; its currency has participated in ERM II for 14 months without tensions; long-term interest rate 1.5 points above the reference value states; Valdarian law allows the finance minister to give instructions to the central bank governor. (a) Name the convergence criteria and where they are laid down. (b) Can Valdaria adopt the euro, and who decides? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – Valdaria fails the public-finance and exchange-rate criteria and the legal convergence requirement; the Council decides under Art 140(2) TFEU.
• Legal basis: Art 140(1) TFEU (four indents) specified by Protocol No 13 on the convergence criteria (and Protocol No 12 on the excessive deficit procedure: 3% deficit / 60% debt reference values).
• Price stability: inflation not more than 1.5 points above the three best performers – 1.1 points: fulfilled.
• Sustainable public finances: no Council decision that an excessive deficit exists (Art 126(6) TFEU) – such a decision exists: NOT fulfilled (the 55% debt alone would be fine).
• Exchange rate: participation in ERM II for at least two years without severe tensions or devaluation – 14 months: NOT fulfilled.
• Long-term interest rates: not more than 2 points above the three best performers – 1.5: fulfilled.
• Legal convergence: national law must be compatible with Arts 130 and 131 TFEU (central bank independence) – ministerial instructions violate Art 130: NOT fulfilled.
• Procedure: Commission and ECB convergence reports (Art 140(1)); Council decision on a Commission proposal after consulting the EP and discussion in the European Council, on a recommendation of a qualified majority of the euro-area members (Art 140(2)); the conversion rate is then fixed irrevocably by the Council with unanimity of the euro states and the state concerned (Art 140(3)).
Codex: Art 140, 126, 130, 131 TFEU · Protocols No 12 and 13.

cards.q: (a) When was the euro introduced as the common currency? (b) Name one measure or instrument created to tackle the euro crisis. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The euro was introduced on 1 January 1999 as book money and on 1 January 2002 as cash; crisis instruments include the European Stability Mechanism (ESM).
• (a) Third stage of EMU on 1 Jan 1999: 11 Member States, conversion rates irrevocably fixed, the ECB conducts the single monetary policy (euro as book/electronic money). Banknotes and coins on 1 Jan 2002 (12 states, Greece having joined in 2001). Today 21 euro states (Croatia 2023, Bulgaria 2026).
• (b) Any one of: ESM (intergovernmental treaty 2012, made possible by the new Art 136(3) TFEU inserted by the simplified revision procedure, Art 48(6) TEU – upheld in Pringle, C-370/12); the temporary EFSF (2010); the Fiscal Compact (TSCG 2012); the Six-Pack and Two-Pack and the European Semester (reinforced economic governance); the Banking Union (Single Supervisory Mechanism with the ECB, Art 127(6) TFEU; Single Resolution Mechanism); the ECB's OMT programme (Gauweiler, C-62/14).
• Correction of a common mistake: the Eurogroup is not a crisis instrument – it pre-dates the crisis (Protocol No 14 on the Euro Group).
Codex: Art 127, 136(3), 140 TFEU; Art 48(6) TEU · Pringle (C-370/12), Gauweiler (C-62/14).

cards.q: Briefly distinguish between the following bodies: the Council of Europe, the European Council, and the Council of the European Union. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only the European Council and the Council (of the EU) are EU institutions; the Council of Europe is a separate international organisation.
• Council of Europe: international organisation founded in 1949 (Statute of London), seat Strasbourg, 46 member states (Russia expelled 2022). Not part of the EU. Main achievement: European Convention on Human Rights (1950) and the European Court of Human Rights. The EU is obliged to accede to the ECHR (Art 6(2) TEU), but has not yet done so (Opinion 2/13).
• European Council (Art 13(1), Art 15 TEU): heads of state or government of the Member States, its own President (2.5 years) and the Commission President; the High Representative takes part. Gives the Union political impetus and defines general political directions and priorities; it 'shall not exercise legislative functions' (Art 15(1) TEU). Decides by consensus unless the Treaties provide otherwise (Art 15(4)).
• Council of the EU, in the Treaties simply 'the Council' (Art 16 TEU): one representative per Member State at ministerial level, authorised to commit the government. Co-legislator and budgetary authority jointly with the EP, policy-making and coordination. Decides by qualified majority as a rule (Art 16(3) TEU); rotating presidency (Art 16(9)).
Codex: Art 13, 15, 16 TEU; Art 6(2) TEU · Opinion 2/13 (ECHR accession).

cards.q: The government of EU Member State Rivaria lowers the retirement age of Supreme Court judges with immediate effect, allowing it to replace one third of the court, and subordinates the prosecution service to the Minister of Justice. (a) Which values of the Union are at stake and where are they laid down? (b) Explain the procedure the Union can use under Art 7 TEU, including who may initiate each step and the majorities required. (c) Rivaria's ally Monturia announces it will veto any sanctions. Does that matter? (d) Can Rivaria challenge an Art 7 decision before the Court of Justice? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The rule of law (Art 2 TEU) is at stake; Art 7 TEU offers a preventive and a sanctioning stage, Monturia can block the determination under Art 7(2), and judicial review is limited to procedure (Art 269 TFEU).
• (a) Art 2 TEU: human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights; judicial independence is part of the rule of law and of effective judicial protection (Art 19(1) second subpara TEU; Art 47 Charter).
• (b) Preventive stage, Art 7(1): on a reasoned proposal of one third of the Member States, the EP or the Commission, the Council, by four fifths of its members, after EP consent, may determine a 'clear risk of a serious breach'; Rivaria must be heard first. Determination of breach, Art 7(2): on a proposal of one third of the Member States or the Commission (not the EP), the European Council by unanimity, after EP consent and Rivaria's observations, may find a 'serious and persistent breach'. Sanctions, Art 7(3): the Council by qualified majority may suspend certain rights, including the voting rights of Rivaria's representative in the Council; Rivaria's obligations remain binding. Art 7(4): variation or revocation by QMV.
• Voting rules, Art 354 TFEU: Rivaria does not vote and is not counted; abstentions do not block unanimity under Art 7(2); the EP consents by two thirds of votes cast representing a majority of its component members.
• (c) Yes. Unanimity in Art 7(2) excludes only the state concerned, so Monturia's vote against blocks the determination and thus any sanction under Art 7(3) (this is why Art 7(1) proceedings against Poland 2017 and Hungary 2018 never reached sanctions). Alternatives: infringement action (Art 258 TFEU; Commission v Poland, C-619/18) based on Art 19(1) TEU (Associação Sindical dos Juízes Portugueses, C-64/16) and the budget Conditionality Regulation 2020/2092 (upheld in C-156/21 Hungary v EP and Council).
• (d) Only as to the procedural stipulations, at Rivaria's request within one month of the determination; the Court rules within one month (Art 269 TFEU).
Codex: Art 2, 7, 19(1) TEU; Art 269, 354, 258 TFEU · C-64/16, C-619/18, C-156/21.

cards.q: The Kingdom of Maghrenia, situated in North Africa, and the Republic of Norland, a European democracy with a market economy, both apply for EU membership. (a) Who may accede under the Treaties and on what conditions? (b) Describe the procedure from application to entry. (c) Can Maghrenia's application succeed? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only a European state that respects and promotes the Art 2 TEU values and meets the Copenhagen criteria can accede under Art 49 TEU; Norland can, Maghrenia cannot.
• (a) Art 49(1) TEU: 'any European State' which respects the values of Art 2 TEU and is committed to promoting them; the conditions of eligibility agreed by the European Council are taken into account – the Copenhagen criteria (1993): political (stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, rule of law, human rights, protection of minorities), economic (functioning market economy able to cope with competitive pressure), acquis (ability to take on the obligations of membership) plus the Union's absorption capacity.
• (b) Application addressed to the Council; the EP and national parliaments are notified; Commission opinion; candidate status; negotiations on the acquis in 35 chapters, each opened and closed unanimously (any Member State can block); at the end the Council decides unanimously after consulting the Commission and after the consent of the EP by a majority of its component members (Art 49(1)); the accession treaty is concluded between the Member States and the applicant and must be ratified by ALL contracting states according to their constitutional requirements (Art 49(2)) – instruments of ratification are deposited with the Italian government. No partial membership.
• (c) Maghrenia is not a 'European State' – Morocco's application of 1987 was rejected on that ground; 'European' is a geographical-political-cultural notion not defined in the Treaties (Cyprus was admitted). Norland's application is admissible; success depends on the political unanimity of all Member States.
Codex: Art 2, 49, 54 TEU (Copenhagen criteria are not in the codex – learn them).

cards.q: After a referendum, Member State Borealis notifies the European Council on 1 March 2025 of its intention to leave the EU. (a) Describe the withdrawal procedure. (b) Negotiations fail and no agreement is concluded. When do the Treaties cease to apply to Borealis, and can this date be postponed? (c) May the Borealian Prime Minister take part in the European Council's deliberations on the negotiating guidelines? (d) In September 2026 a new Borealian government wants to stay in the EU. Can it unilaterally revoke the notification? (e) Could Borealis later rejoin? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under Art 50 TEU the Treaties cease to apply two years after notification (1 March 2027) unless an agreement enters into force earlier or the European Council unanimously extends the period; Borealis does not participate; revocation is possible (Wightman); re-entry only under Art 49.
• (a) Decision to withdraw in accordance with the state's own constitutional requirements (Art 50(1)); notification to the European Council, which adopts guidelines; the Union negotiates the withdrawal agreement under Art 218(3) TFEU; the Council concludes it by qualified majority after obtaining the EP's consent (Art 50(2)).
• (b) Without an agreement the Treaties cease to apply two years after the notification, i.e. on 1 March 2027 (Art 50(3)), unless the European Council, in agreement with Borealis, unanimously extends that period (Brexit: notification 29 March 2017, extensions, exit 31 January 2020).
• (c) No. The member of the European Council or Council representing the withdrawing state does not participate in its discussions or decisions concerning withdrawal (Art 50(4)); QMV is then defined by Art 238(3)(b) TFEU – 72% of the remaining members (19 of 26) representing 65% of their population.
• (d) Yes, still possible because the two-year period has not expired and no agreement is in force: the CJEU held in Wightman (C-621/18, 2018) that a state may revoke its notification unilaterally, provided the revocation is unequivocal and unconditional, communicated in writing to the European Council and decided in accordance with its constitutional requirements.
• (e) Yes, but only by applying under the Art 49 procedure like any other state (Art 50(5)).
Codex: Art 50, 49 TEU; Art 218(3), 238(3)(b) TFEU · Wightman (C-621/18).

cards.q: Explain the principle of sincere cooperation (loyalty). Where is it laid down, what obligations does it contain, and give three examples of how the Court of Justice has used it. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 4(3) TEU obliges the Union and the Member States to assist each other and the Member States to take all appropriate measures to fulfil EU obligations and to refrain from anything that could jeopardise the Union's objectives.
• Content (Art 4(3) TEU): (1) mutual assistance in full mutual respect – it binds both the Member States and the Union institutions; (2) positive duty: 'any appropriate measure, general or particular' to ensure fulfilment of obligations arising from the Treaties or from acts of the institutions; (3) negative duty: refrain from any measure which could jeopardise the attainment of the Union's objectives.
• Examples from case law: duty of national courts to interpret national law in conformity with directives (von Colson, 14/83); duty to penalise breaches of EU law by effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions (Greek Maize, 68/88); duty not to adopt measures seriously compromising a directive's result during the transposition period (Inter-Environnement Wallonie, C-129/96); state liability (Francovich, C-6/90); a supporting argument for primacy (Costa v ENEL, 6/64); unity of external representation.
• In an infringement action Art 4(3) is usually invoked together with the specific obligation breached.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU (also Art 291(1) TFEU) · von Colson, Inter-Environnement Wallonie, Francovich, Costa v ENEL.

cards.q: A Japanese company claims that it can only conclude a trade agreement with 'the Member States', since the EU is 'a mere association of states without personality'. Separately, an Austrian supplier wants to sue the EU in an Austrian court for an unpaid invoice under a supply contract. Assess both claims. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both claims are wrong – the EU has international legal personality (Art 47 TEU) and legal capacity in national law (Art 335 TFEU), and contractual disputes go to national courts unless there is an arbitration clause.
• Art 47 TEU: 'The Union shall have legal personality.' Since Lisbon the Union has replaced and succeeded the EC, which already had personality (Art 1(3) TEU). Consequences: the Union concludes international agreements in its own name (Art 216 TFEU; common commercial policy is even exclusive, Art 3(1)(e) TFEU), is a member of international organisations (e.g. WTO, FAO), must accede to the ECHR (Art 6(2) TEU), has privileges and immunities (Art 343 TFEU, Protocol No 7).
• Art 335 TFEU: in each Member State the Union enjoys the most extensive legal capacity accorded to legal persons – it may acquire property and be a party to legal proceedings, represented by the Commission (or by the institution concerned).
• Contract claim: contractual liability is governed by the law applicable to the contract (Art 340(1) TFEU); disputes to which the Union is a party are not excluded from national courts' jurisdiction (Art 274 TFEU); the CJEU has jurisdiction only under an arbitration clause (Art 272 TFEU). So the Austrian court can hear the case, subject to immunity from execution (Protocol No 7).
Codex: Art 47, 1(3), 6(2) TEU; Art 216, 272, 274, 335, 340(1), 343 TFEU.

cards.q: (a) Did the EEC Treaty in its original version contain a written catalogue of fundamental rights? (b) On what basis did the Court of Justice develop its fundamental-rights case law? Name well-known judgments. (c) How did the Treaty of Lisbon change the legal situation? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No catalogue existed; the Court developed fundamental rights as unwritten general principles of law (Stauder, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Nold); since Lisbon the Charter is binding primary law (Art 6(1) TEU).
• (a) No. The EEC Treaty (1957) was an economic treaty; it contained only specific guarantees such as non-discrimination on nationality and equal pay. Early on the Court refused to review Community acts against national fundamental rights (Stork, 1/58).
• (b) General principles of Community law, which the Court 'ensures': Stauder (29/69, 1969) – fundamental rights are enshrined in the general principles; Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70, 1970) – inspired by the constitutional traditions common to the Member States (while EU law prevails over national constitutions); Nold (4/73, 1974) – also international human-rights treaties, above all the ECHR; Hauer (44/79). Driver: pressure from national constitutional courts (Solange I, 1974). Codified by Maastricht (Art F(2) TEU).
• (c) Lisbon: the Charter of Fundamental Rights (proclaimed Nice 2000) has 'the same legal value as the Treaties' (Art 6(1) TEU) = primary law; it does not extend Union competences (Art 6(1) subpara 2, Art 51(2) Charter) and binds Member States only when implementing Union law (Art 51(1) Charter; Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10); obligation to accede to the ECHR (Art 6(2) TEU); general principles remain a source (Art 6(3) TEU).
Codex: Art 6 TEU; Art 51–53 Charter · Stauder, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Nold, Åkerberg Fransson.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Explain the composition, functions and decision-making of the European Council. Since when is it an institution of the Union? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The European Council (Art 15 TEU) is the body of the heads of state or government that gives political direction without legislating, decides by consensus, and has been an institution only since Lisbon (2009).
• Composition (Art 15(2) TEU): heads of state or government of the Member States, its President and the President of the Commission; the High Representative takes part. Meets twice every six months, convened by its President (Art 15(3)).
• President (Art 15(5)–(6)): elected by the European Council by qualified majority for two and a half years, renewable once; chairs and drives forward the work, reports to the EP after each meeting, represents the Union externally in CFSP matters at his level; may not hold a national office (Costa, since 1 Dec 2024).
• Functions (Art 15(1)): provides impetus and defines general political directions and priorities; 'shall not exercise legislative functions'. In addition: recruitment (proposes the Commission President, Art 17(7); appoints the High Representative, Art 18(1)); constitutional architect (Art 48 TEU revisions and passerelles); Art 7(2) TEU determination; Art 50 guidelines and extension; arbitration in emergency-brake cases.
• Decision-making (Art 15(4)): consensus unless the Treaties provide otherwise (QMV e.g. Art 15(5), 17(7); unanimity e.g. Art 7(2), 48(6)); its President and the Commission President do not vote (Art 235(1) TFEU).
• History: informal summits from 1974, recognised by the Single European Act 1986, listed as an institution in Art 13(1) TEU since the Treaty of Lisbon.
Codex: Art 13(1), 15, 17(7), 18(1) TEU; Art 235, 236 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Facing a migration emergency, the European Council at its summit adopts by consensus a 'Regulation on the mandatory relocation of asylum seekers', binding on all Member States. Member State Pannonia, whose Prime Minister was absent, considers the act unlawful. (a) Was the European Council entitled to adopt this act? (b) What can Pannonia do? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – the European Council has no legislative function (Art 15(1) TEU); Pannonia can bring an action for annulment for lack of competence.
• (a) Art 15(1) TEU: the European Council 'shall not exercise legislative functions'. Legislative acts are adopted by the EP and the Council on a Commission proposal (Art 14(1), 16(1), 17(2) TEU; Art 289, 294 TFEU). The correct basis would be Art 78(2) TFEU (OLP) or, for an emergency, Art 78(3) TFEU (provisional measures by the Council on a Commission proposal after consulting the EP) – the 2015 relocation decision was adopted exactly that way and upheld (Slovakia and Hungary v Council, C-643/15 and C-647/15). Each institution must act within the powers conferred on it (Art 13(2) TEU, institutional balance). Consensus does not cure the lack of competence.
• (b) Since Lisbon, acts of the European Council intended to produce legal effects vis-à-vis third parties are reviewable (Art 263(1) TFEU). Pannonia is a privileged applicant (Art 263(2)), must sue within two months (Art 263(6)), ground: lack of competence; the Court declares the act void (Art 264). Note: mere political conclusions of the European Council are not challengeable, since they produce no legal effects.
Codex: Art 13(2), 15(1) TEU; Art 78, 263, 264 TFEU · C-643/15 and C-647/15.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. Justify your answer. (a) 'The permanent President of the Council has voting rights in the European Council.' (b) 'The President of the European Council may at the same time remain Prime Minister of his home state.' (c) 'The European Council always decides unanimously.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false.
• (a) False on two levels. The Council of the EU has no permanent President: its configurations are chaired by Member States on the basis of equal rotation for six months (Art 16(9) TEU, Art 236(b) TFEU), except the Foreign Affairs Council, chaired by the High Representative (Art 18(3) TEU). If the statement means the permanent President of the European Council (Art 15(5) TEU): when the European Council votes, its President and the Commission President do not take part in the vote (Art 235(1) TFEU).
• (b) False. The President of the European Council 'shall not hold a national office' (Art 15(6) last sentence TEU) – Charles Michel had to resign as Belgian Prime Minister.
• (c) False. The rule is consensus (Art 15(4) TEU), which is not a formal unanimous vote. Where the Treaties provide otherwise it votes: qualified majority (election of its President, Art 15(5); proposal of the Commission President, Art 17(7); list of Council configurations, Art 236 TFEU), unanimity (e.g. Art 7(2), 48(6), 50(3) TEU), simple majority (procedural questions, Art 235(3) TFEU; Art 48(3) TEU). Abstentions do not prevent unanimity (Art 235(1) TFEU).
Codex: Art 15, 16(9), 18(3) TEU; Art 235, 236 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Name and explain four tasks of the European Commission, each with its legal basis. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Initiative (monopoly), guardian of the Treaties, executive/budget, and external representation – all rooted in Art 17(1)–(2) TEU.
• 1. Right of initiative: it promotes the general interest of the Union and takes initiatives; legislative acts may only be adopted on the basis of a Commission proposal unless the Treaties provide otherwise (Art 17(2) TEU; Art 294(2) TFEU); it also initiates annual and multiannual programming (Commission Work Programme) and submits the draft budget (Art 314(2) TFEU).
• 2. Guardian of the Treaties: it ensures the application of the Treaties and of measures adopted by the institutions and oversees the application of Union law under the control of the CJEU (Art 17(1) TEU) – infringement procedure (Art 258, 260(2) TFEU), supervision of state aid (Art 108 TFEU) and of the competition rules (Art 105 TFEU), monitoring of national budgets (Art 126(2) TFEU).
• 3. Executive and management functions: executes the budget and manages programmes (Art 317 TFEU), adopts delegated and implementing acts (Art 290, 291(2) TFEU), coordinating and management functions.
• 4. External representation: represents the Union externally except in the CFSP and other cases provided by the Treaties (Art 17(1) TEU); negotiates international agreements, e.g. trade agreements (Art 207(3), 218(3) TFEU).
Codex: Art 17(1)–(2) TEU; Art 105, 108, 126, 207, 218, 258, 290, 291, 294(2), 314, 317 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: (1) The European Parliament, by a majority of its component members, asks the Commission to propose a directive on a 'right to disconnect' for workers. (2) A European citizens' initiative 'Save the Bees' collects 1.2 million signatures from nine Member States asking for a ban on certain pesticides. The Commission does not want to act. Is it obliged to submit a legislative proposal in either case? Could the Parliament or the Council simply adopt the act without a proposal? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – the Commission's monopoly of initiative (Art 17(2) TEU) means it only has to state its reasons; without a Commission proposal the legislators cannot adopt the act.
• Monopoly: Union legislative acts may only be adopted on the basis of a Commission proposal, except where the Treaties provide otherwise (Art 17(2) TEU). Exceptions: a quarter of the Member States in police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters (Art 76 TFEU); cases under Art 289(4) TFEU (group of Member States, EP, ECB, CJEU, EIB); CFSP initiatives by Member States or the High Representative (Art 30 TEU).
• (1) Indirect initiative of the EP, Art 225 TFEU: the EP may request a proposal; if the Commission does not submit one, it 'shall inform the European Parliament of the reasons' – no legal duty to propose (same for the Council, Art 241 TFEU).
• (2) European citizens' initiative, Art 11(4) TEU, Art 24 TFEU, Regulation 2019/788: at least one million citizens from at least a quarter of the Member States (7) – fulfilled. Consequences: the Commission meets the organisers, the EP holds a public hearing, and the Commission sets out within six months in a communication its conclusions, the action it intends to take and its reasons. It is not obliged to propose (Puppinck, C-418/18 P).
• Neither the EP nor the Council can act in its place; an act adopted without the required proposal would be annulled (Art 263(2) TFEU).
Codex: Art 11(4), 17(2), 30 TEU; Art 24, 76, 225, 241, 289(4), 293 TFEU · Puppinck (C-418/18 P).

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Commissioner Novak receives a letter from the Prime Minister of his home state instructing him to vote against a Commission decision on state aid to a national airline; he complies. At the same time some Member States propose reducing the Commission to 18 members. (a) Assess Novak's conduct and its possible consequences. (b) How many Commissioners are there and can their number be reduced? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Novak breached his duty of independence (Art 17(3) TEU, Art 245 TFEU); there is one Commissioner per Member State under a European Council decision, which could be changed only by unanimity.
• (a) Art 17(3) TEU: the Commission is completely independent; its members 'shall neither seek nor take instructions from any Government'. Member States must respect this independence and not seek to influence Commissioners (Art 245(1) TFEU). Consequences: the President may request his resignation, which he must then tender (Art 17(6) TEU); on application by the Council (simple majority) or the Commission, the Court of Justice may compulsorily retire him for serious misconduct (Art 247 TFEU) or deprive him of pension rights for breach of his obligations (Art 245(2) TFEU; Commission v Cresson, C-432/04). The Commission decision itself remains a collegiate act.
• (b) Composition: Commissioners are chosen for general competence, European commitment and independence beyond doubt; term five years (Art 17(3)). Since 1 Nov 2014 the Treaty provides for two thirds of the number of Member States 'unless the European Council, acting unanimously, decides to alter this number' (Art 17(5)); the European Council did so (Decision 2013/272/EU, following the guarantee given to Ireland), so there is one national per Member State (27, including the President and the High Representative). A reduction to 18 would require a new unanimous European Council decision and strictly equal rotation (Art 17(5), Art 244 TFEU).
Codex: Art 17(3), (5), (6) TEU; Art 244, 245, 247 TFEU · Cresson (C-432/04).

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: After the European elections, the party alliance 'Alpha' becomes the largest group in the European Parliament; its lead candidate (Spitzenkandidat) is Mr Berger. The European Council, by qualified majority, instead proposes Ms Lind, who did not run as a lead candidate. (a) Is this lawful? (b) Describe the further steps until the Commission takes office. (c) What happens if the Parliament rejects Ms Lind? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Lawful – Art 17(7) TEU only requires the European Council to 'take into account' the election results; the Spitzenkandidaten process is political practice, not law.
• (a) Art 17(7) first subpara TEU: 'Taking into account the elections to the European Parliament and after having held the appropriate consultations', the European Council, by QMV, proposes a candidate (see also Declaration No 11). There is no legal obligation to nominate a lead candidate. The practice was followed in 2014 (Juncker), ignored in 2019 (von der Leyen was not a lead candidate) and followed again in 2024 (von der Leyen as EPP lead candidate).
• (b) The EP elects the candidate by a majority of its component members (at least 361 of 720). The Council, by common accord with the President-elect, adopts the list of the other Commissioners on the basis of the Member States' suggestions (Art 17(7) second subpara); the High Representative is appointed by the European Council by QMV with the President's agreement (Art 18(1)). The Commissioners-designate are heard by EP committees (candidates may be withdrawn). The Commission as a body is subject to a vote of consent by the EP, then appointed by the European Council by QMV (Art 17(7) third subpara).
• (c) If she does not obtain the required majority, the European Council, by QMV, proposes a new candidate within one month, following the same procedure (Art 17(7) first subpara). The EP thus has a veto but no right to impose its own candidate.
Codex: Art 14(1), 17(3), 17(7), 18(1) TEU · Declaration No 11 on Art 17(6) and (7) TEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: The 'Ned-Leaks' revelations show that the Netherlands operated tax-avoidance schemes distorting competition in the EU. Commission President Niederknaaken was Dutch finance minister when the schemes were set up. (a) Does the European Parliament have the power to remove President Niederknaaken? (b) A motion of censure is tabled; 540 MEPs vote, 370 in favour. Is it carried? What if 500 MEPs had voted and 350 had voted in favour? (c) What other options exist? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The EP cannot remove the President alone; it can only censure the whole Commission (Art 17(8) TEU, Art 234 TFEU) – carried in the first vote, not in the second.
• (a) The Commission as a body is responsible to the EP (Art 17(8) TEU). The only binding instrument is the motion of censure against the college: if carried, the members of the Commission 'shall resign as a body' and the High Representative resigns from her duties in the Commission (Art 234(2) TFEU). There is no motion against the President or a single Commissioner.
• (b) Art 234 TFEU: vote no earlier than three days after tabling, by open vote; majority required: two thirds of the votes cast AND a majority of the component members (361 of 720). 370 of 540 = 68.5% (≥ two thirds) and 370 ≥ 361 → carried. 350 of 500 = 70%, but 350 < 361 → not carried. If carried, the Commission continues to deal with current business until replaced; the new Commission's term ends when the censured one's would have ended.
• (c) Voluntary resignation (Art 246 TFEU); compulsory retirement by the Court of Justice for serious misconduct or no longer fulfilling the conditions – but only on application of the Council or the Commission, not the EP (Art 247 TFEU); political control – questions (Art 230 TFEU), a committee of inquiry into maladministration in implementing Union law (Art 226 TFEU), resolutions. Real parallel: after LuxLeaks a censure motion against the Juncker Commission (2014) failed; no censure motion has ever been carried (the Santer Commission resigned in 1999 before a vote).
Codex: Art 14(1), 17(8) TEU; Art 226, 230, 234, 246, 247 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Commissioner Dalberg is involved in a lobbying scandal. The European Parliament adopts a resolution demanding his dismissal, but the Commission President refuses to act. What legal means exist to end Dalberg's term, and who may use them? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only the President (request to resign, Art 17(6) TEU) or the Court of Justice (compulsory retirement, Art 247 TFEU, on application of the Council or the Commission) can end an individual Commissioner's term; the EP's resolution is not binding.
• Art 17(6) second subpara TEU: 'A member of the Commission shall resign if the President so requests' – the decision lies with the President, reflecting her leadership of the college (Art 17(6)(a)–(c)).
• Art 247 TFEU: if a member no longer fulfils the conditions required for his duties or is guilty of serious misconduct, the Court of Justice may, on application by the Council (simple majority) or the Commission, compulsorily retire him. Art 245(2): breach of the obligations of office can also lead to deprivation of pension rights (Cresson, C-432/04).
• EP: no individual censure. Under the Framework Agreement EP–Commission (2010), if the EP asks the President to withdraw confidence in a member, she must seriously consider it and either request the resignation or explain her refusal to the EP – politically, not legally, binding. The EP's only binding sanction is censure of the whole college (Art 17(8) TEU, Art 234 TFEU).
• Vacancy: replaced by the Council by common accord with the President after consulting the EP (Art 246 TFEU). Real example: Commissioner Dalli resigned in 2012 at President Barroso's request.
Codex: Art 17(6), 17(8) TEU; Art 234, 245, 246, 247 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false: 'The Commission can, contrary to the principle that enforcement of Union law is the responsibility of the Member States, directly enforce Union law itself.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: True – as an exception to decentralised (indirect) enforcement, the Commission itself enforces Union law against undertakings and Member States in certain fields.
• Principle: Union law is as a rule implemented and enforced by the Member States – their authorities and courts (Art 4(3) TEU, Art 291(1) TFEU, Art 19(1) second subpara TEU; procedural autonomy limited by equivalence and effectiveness).
• Exceptions – direct (centralised) enforcement by the Commission: competition law – Arts 101 and 102 TFEU, Art 105 TFEU and Regulation 1/2003 (inspections, decisions, fines up to 10% of turnover); merger control (Regulation 139/2004); state aid – Commission decisions under Art 108(2) TFEU ordering recovery; management of Union funds and execution of the budget (Art 317 TFEU); implementing acts where uniform conditions are needed (Art 291(2) TFEU).
• Note: receiving a complaint is not direct enforcement; the infringement procedure (Art 258 TFEU) is supervision of Member States, which the Commission opens at its discretion.
Codex: Art 4(3), 17(1) TEU; Art 105, 108, 258, 291, 317 TFEU · Regulation 1/2003 (not in the codex).

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: How does the Commission take its decisions, and how does this differ from the European Council? What does the principle of collegiality mean? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Commission decides as a college by a majority of its members (Art 250 TFEU); the European Council decides by consensus (Art 15(4) TEU).
• Commission: acts by a majority of its members, i.e. an absolute majority of the component members (14 of 27), with a quorum of the majority of members under its Rules of Procedure (Art 250 TFEU); in practice mostly consensus. Collegiality: every decision is attributed to the college as a whole and all members bear collective political responsibility (hence censure only of the whole college, Art 17(8) TEU); no department principle. Practical procedures: oral meetings, written procedure, empowerment of a single Commissioner for management measures and delegation – accepted by the Court as long as the college keeps responsibility (AKZO, 5/85). The President lays down guidelines and decides on internal organisation (Art 17(6) TEU).
• European Council: presence quorum two thirds; decisions by consensus unless the Treaties provide otherwise; President and Commission President do not vote (Art 235(1) TFEU).
Codex: Art 15(4), 17(6), 17(8) TEU; Art 235, 250 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Describe the Council of the European Union: its composition, configurations, presidency and the role of Coreper. Then comment on the statement: 'The Council negotiates and adopts legislation behind closed doors, and the same minister always represents a Member State.' (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Council is one institution of national ministers meeting in configurations, chaired by a six-monthly rotating presidency and prepared by Coreper; the statement is false.
• Composition (Art 16(2) TEU): a representative of each Member State at ministerial level who may commit the government and cast its vote. Functions (Art 16(1)): jointly with the EP legislative and budgetary functions; policy-making and coordinating functions.
• Configurations (Art 16(6) TEU, Art 236 TFEU): e.g. General Affairs (ensures consistency, prepares European Council meetings), Foreign Affairs, ECOFIN, Justice and Home Affairs, Agriculture and Fisheries, Competitiveness, Environment – ten in total, but legally one institution. The Euro Group is an informal meeting of euro-area ministers (Art 137 TFEU, Protocol No 14).
• Presidency (Art 16(9) TEU, Art 236(b) TFEU): Member States hold it for six months on the basis of equal rotation, in trios for continuity; the presidency is a broker. Exception: the Foreign Affairs Council is chaired by the High Representative (Art 18(3) TEU).
• Coreper (Art 16(7) TEU, Art 240(1) TFEU): Committee of Permanent Representatives – Coreper II (ambassadors: GAC, FAC, ECOFIN, JHA) and Coreper I (deputies: more technical files) – with about 150–250 working parties; it prepares the agenda: 'A items' adopted without debate, 'B items' discussed by ministers. General Secretariat (Art 240(2)).
• Statement false: the Council meets in public when it deliberates and votes on a draft legislative act (Art 16(8) TEU; Art 15(2) TFEU); and which minister attends depends on the configuration (e.g. the environment minister in ENVI).
Codex: Art 16, 18(3) TEU; Art 15(2), 236, 237, 240 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: The Council votes on three Commission proposals under the ordinary legislative procedure (27 Member States). Was each proposal adopted? (a) 16 Member States representing 63% of the EU population vote in favour, the other 11 against. (b) 14 Member States representing 72% of the population vote in favour. (c) 24 Member States representing 53% of the population vote in favour; the three most populous states, representing about 47%, vote against. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) not adopted, (b) not adopted, (c) adopted – because a blocking minority needs at least four members.
• Rule (Art 16(3)–(4) TEU, Art 238(3) TFEU for special cases): QMV requires at least 55% of the members of the Council, comprising at least 15 of them, representing Member States comprising at least 65% of the Union population (double majority). A blocking minority must include at least four Council members, failing which the qualified majority is deemed attained (Art 16(4) second subpara).
• (a) States: 16 ≥ 15 – met. Population: 63% < 65% – not met. The 11 opponents (37%, more than 4 states) form a valid blocking minority → NOT adopted.
• (b) Population 72% – met; states 14 < 15 (55% of 27 = 14.85, rounded up) → NOT adopted, despite the large population share.
• (c) Population 53% < 65%, but only three states oppose. A blocking minority requires at least four members → the qualified majority is 'deemed attained' → ADOPTED. The rule prevents the three largest states from blocking on their own.
• Remember: abstentions count as not voting in favour, so in QMV an abstention works like a 'no'.
Codex: Art 16(3)–(4) TEU; Art 238 TFEU; Protocol No 36 (transitional rules, expired).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: (a) A directive harmonising turnover taxes under Art 113 TFEU (unanimity) is put to the vote: 25 Member States vote in favour, Malta abstains and Ireland votes against. Is it adopted? What if Ireland had also abstained? (b) Which majority applies when the Council decides on an initiative presented by a quarter of the Member States in police cooperation (Art 76(b) TFEU)? (c) Which majority applies in the Council when only the 16 states participating in an enhanced cooperation vote? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No – Ireland's 'no' is a veto, but two abstentions would not block; (b) reinforced QMV of 72% (Art 238(2) TFEU); (c) QMV calculated among participating states (Art 238(3)(a) TFEU).
• (a) Unanimity means no member votes against. Art 238(4) TFEU: abstentions by members present in person or represented do not prevent the adoption of acts requiring unanimity. So with Ireland against → not adopted; with Malta and Ireland abstaining → adopted. (A member may act on behalf of only one other member, Art 239 TFEU.)
• (b) Where the Council does not act on a proposal from the Commission or the High Representative, QMV is at least 72% of the members (20 of 27) representing at least 65% of the population (Art 238(2) TFEU) – the stricter threshold compensates for the missing Commission proposal.
• (c) Where not all members vote (enhanced cooperation, Art 330 TFEU; euro-area measures; Art 7 and Art 50 TEU): at least 55% of the participating members representing at least 65% of their population; blocking minority = at least the minimum number of members representing more than 35% of the participating states' population, plus one member (Art 238(3)(a)); 72% if not on a Commission proposal (Art 238(3)(b)).
• Simple majority, for procedural matters: majority of the component members, i.e. 14 (Art 238(1), 240(3) TFEU).
Codex: Art 16(4) TEU; Art 76, 113, 238, 239, 240(3), 330 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: After a census Germany's population has grown. The German government demands 110 seats in the European Parliament, Malta insists on keeping its 6 seats, and the European Council decides by qualified majority to enlarge the Parliament to 760 members. Assess the legality. What does 'degressive proportionality' mean? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Unlawful – Art 14(2) TEU caps the Parliament at 750 members plus the President and each state at 96 seats (minimum 6), and the composition decision requires unanimity on the EP's initiative and with its consent.
• Art 14(2) TEU: MEPs are representatives of the Union's citizens; their number shall not exceed 750, plus the President. Representation is degressively proportional, with a minimum threshold of six members per Member State and no state allocated more than 96 seats.
• Degressive proportionality: larger states have more seats than smaller ones, but each MEP from a larger state represents more citizens (a Maltese MEP represents far fewer inhabitants than a German one).
• Application: 110 seats for Germany exceed the maximum of 96; Malta's 6 seats are the minimum and cannot be reduced; 760 exceeds 750 + 1 – only a Treaty amendment could change these limits.
• Procedure: the European Council adopts the composition decision unanimously, on the initiative of the EP and with its consent (Art 14(2) second subpara) – QMV is insufficient. Current decision: 720 MEPs for 2024–2029 (Germany 96, Austria 20, Malta 6).
• Election: direct universal suffrage, free and secret ballot, five-year term (Art 14(3) TEU), since 1979; EU citizens may vote and stand where they reside (Art 22(2) TFEU; Art 39 Charter).
Codex: Art 14(2)–(3) TEU; Art 22, 223 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Explain the powers of the European Parliament. Distinguish its legislative, budgetary and supervisory (control) functions and give the relevant Treaty provisions. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 14(1) TEU gives the EP legislative and budgetary functions jointly with the Council, functions of political control and consultation, and the election of the Commission President.
• Legislative: co-legislator on an equal footing with the Council in the ordinary legislative procedure (Art 289(1), 294 TFEU); in special procedures either consent (e.g. Art 19, 312(2), 352 TFEU) or mere consultation (e.g. Art 113, 115 TFEU; failure to consult annuls the act – Roquette Frères, 138/79); indirect right of initiative (Art 225 TFEU).
• Budgetary: adopts the annual budget jointly with the Council and can reject it (Art 314 TFEU); consent to the multiannual financial framework by a majority of its component members (Art 312(2)); grants discharge to the Commission on the Council's recommendation (Art 319).
• Supervisory/political control: elects the Commission President and gives consent to the college (Art 17(7) TEU); motion of censure (Art 17(8) TEU, Art 234 TFEU); questions – the Commission must reply orally or in writing (Art 230 TFEU); debate of the annual general report (Art 233); temporary committees of inquiry at the request of a quarter of its members (Art 226); petitions (Art 227, Art 24 TFEU); elects the European Ombudsman (Art 228); objections to delegated acts (Art 290(2)); privileged applicant in annulment and failure-to-act actions (Art 263(2), 265).
• Consent in constitutional and external matters: international agreements (Art 218(6)(a) TFEU), accession (Art 49 TEU), withdrawal (Art 50(2) TEU), Art 7 TEU, enhanced cooperation (Art 329(1) TFEU), passerelle (Art 48(7) TEU).
• Limit: no censure power over the European Council or the Council, whose members answer to national parliaments (Art 10(2) TEU).
Codex: Art 10(2), 14, 17(7)–(8) TEU; Art 225–234, 263, 290, 294, 312, 314, 319 TFEU · Roquette Frères (138/79).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. Justify your answer. (a) 'In addition to its legislative function, the European Parliament also has an oversight role with regard to other Union institutions.' (b) 'The European Parliament can force the Council to resign by a motion of censure.' (c) 'An EP committee of inquiry may investigate alleged maladministration in a matter currently pending before a national court.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) true, (b) false, (c) false.
• (a) True. Art 14(1) TEU gives the EP 'functions of political control'. Main addressee is the Commission: election of its President and consent to the college (Art 17(7) TEU), censure (Art 17(8) TEU, Art 234 TFEU), questions (Art 230 TFEU), discharge (Art 319 TFEU), committees of inquiry (Art 226 TFEU). Weaker control of others: the European Council President reports after each meeting (Art 15(6)(d) TEU); the ECB presents its annual report and its President may be heard by EP committees (Art 284(3) TFEU); the EP elects the Ombudsman (Art 228 TFEU).
• (b) False. Censure exists only against the Commission (Art 17(8) TEU). Council members are democratically accountable to their national parliaments or citizens (Art 10(2) TEU); the EP has no such power over the Council or the European Council.
• (c) False. Art 226(1) TFEU: a committee of inquiry investigates alleged contraventions or maladministration in the implementation of Union law 'except where the alleged facts are being examined before a court and while the case is still subject to legal proceedings'.
Codex: Art 10(2), 14(1), 15(6), 17(7)–(8) TEU; Art 226, 228, 230, 234, 284(3), 319 TFEU.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Describe the structure of the Court of Justice of the European Union. Then comment on the statement: 'The Court of Justice of the EU is supported by a number of agencies and offices (e.g. for aviation safety) that are assigned to it in varying degrees.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The CJEU consists of the Court of Justice, the General Court and (possible) specialised courts (Art 19(1) TEU); the statement is false – agencies such as EASA are not part of the CJEU but are subject to its review.
• Mission (Art 19(1) TEU): to ensure that in the interpretation and application of the Treaties the law is observed; Member States provide remedies for effective legal protection.
• Court of Justice: one judge per Member State (27), assisted by eleven Advocates General (Art 19(2) TEU, Art 252 TFEU); hears preliminary references, infringement actions, most actions by Member States and institutions, and appeals.
• General Court: at least one judge per Member State (Art 19(2)), currently two per state; first instance for annulment, failure to act, damages actions by individuals (Art 256(1) TFEU), with appeal on points of law to the Court of Justice; since October 2024 also preliminary rulings in certain specific areas (Art 256(3)).
• Specialised courts (Art 257 TFEU): may be attached to the General Court by EP and Council under the OLP; the only one, the Civil Service Tribunal (2005–2016), was abolished – none exists today.
• The statement: the European Union Aviation Safety Agency is a decentralised agency set up by secondary law and belongs to the executive side; agencies are not 'assigned' to the Court. On the contrary, the CJEU reviews the legality of their acts intended to produce legal effects (Art 263(1), (5) TFEU; also Art 265, 267(1)(b), 277).
Codex: Art 19 TEU; Art 251–257, 263, 267 TFEU; Protocol No 3 (Statute of the CJEU).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: (a) According to which criteria are the judges and Advocates General of the Court of Justice selected, and how are they appointed? (b) What is the role of the Advocates General? (c) Member State Ostland nominates its former justice minister, whom the panel under Art 255 TFEU considers unsuitable. Can the governments nevertheless appoint him? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Independence beyond doubt plus the highest judicial qualifications (Art 19(2) TEU, Art 253 TFEU); AGs deliver independent, non-binding reasoned opinions (Art 252 TFEU); the panel's opinion is mandatory to obtain but not formally binding.
• (a) Judges and AGs of the Court of Justice: persons whose independence is beyond doubt and who possess the qualifications required for appointment to the highest judicial offices in their countries or are jurisconsults of recognised competence (Art 253(1) TFEU; Art 19(2) third subpara TEU). Appointed by common accord of the governments of the Member States for six years, after consultation of the Art 255 panel; partial replacement every three years; reappointment possible. General Court judges: independence beyond doubt and ability required for high judicial office (Art 254(2)).
• (b) Art 252(2) TFEU: acting with complete impartiality and independence, the AG makes, in open court, reasoned submissions (Opinions) on cases requiring his involvement; not binding but influential; no Opinion needed if no new point of law (Art 20 Statute). Eleven AGs (Art 252(1) as increased by the Council).
• (c) The seven-member panel (former CJEU members, national supreme-court judges, renowned lawyers, one proposed by the EP) must be consulted (Art 255), but its opinion is not formally binding – appointment by common accord remains legally possible; in practice rejected candidates have always been withdrawn.
Codex: Art 19(2) TEU; Art 252–255 TFEU; Protocol No 3 (Statute), Art 20.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: The finance minister of euro-area state Aldora instructs the governor of the Aldoran central bank to vote in the ECB Governing Council for lower interest rates. The Aldoran parliament also demands that the ECB buy Aldoran government bonds directly at issue. Assess both under EU law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both are incompatible with EU law – the instruction breaches ECB/central bank independence (Art 130 TFEU) and direct bond purchases breach the prohibition of monetary financing (Art 123 TFEU).
• Status: the ECB is an institution (Art 13(1) TEU) with legal personality; with the national central banks it forms the ESCB, and with the euro-area central banks the Eurosystem, which conducts monetary policy (Art 282 TFEU). Primary objective: price stability; without prejudice to that, it supports the Union's general economic policies (Art 127(1) TFEU); tasks: monetary policy, foreign-exchange operations, reserves, payment systems (Art 127(2)).
• Independence (Art 130 TFEU): neither the ECB, nor a national central bank, nor any member of their decision-making bodies may seek or take instructions from Union institutions or national governments; governments undertake not to seek to influence them. The minister's instruction is unlawful; national law must be compatible (Art 131). The governor's term is protected (Statute Art 14.2; Rimšēvičs, C-202/18).
• Art 123 TFEU prohibits overdraft facilities and the direct purchase of debt instruments from Member States by the ECB or national central banks. Purchases on secondary markets are permissible only within limits (Gauweiler, C-62/14; Weiss, C-493/17).
• Organs: Governing Council and Executive Board (six members appointed by the European Council by QMV for eight non-renewable years, Art 283 TFEU); seat Frankfurt.
Codex: Art 13(1) TEU; Art 123, 127, 130, 131, 282–284 TFEU · Gauweiler (C-62/14), Weiss (C-493/17).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'The European Court of Auditors can annul unlawful expenditure and fine the Member States responsible.' (b) 'The European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions are institutions of the Union.' (c) 'A directive adopted without consulting the Committee of the Regions, although the legal basis requires consultation, is valid, since its opinions are not binding anyway.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false.
• (a) False. The Court of Auditors is an institution (Art 13(1) TEU) but has no judicial or sanctioning powers. It examines the accounts of all revenue and expenditure of the Union and of its bodies (Art 287(1) TFEU) – financial, compliance and performance audits – provides the EP and Council with a statement of assurance on the reliability of the accounts and the legality and regularity of transactions, publishes an annual report (Art 287(4)) and assists them in controlling the budget (discharge, Art 319). Suspected fraud goes to OLAF / the EPPO. One member per state, appointed by the Council after consulting the EP for six years (Art 285, 286(2)).
• (b) False. They are advisory bodies assisting the EP, Council and Commission (Art 13(4) TEU, Art 300 TFEU). EESC: representatives of employers, employees and other civil-society organisations (Art 300(2), 301–304); CoR: representatives of regional and local bodies holding an electoral mandate or politically accountable to an elected assembly (Art 300(3), 305–307); each at most 350 members, appointed by the Council for five years.
• (c) False. The opinion is non-binding, but mandatory consultation is an essential procedural requirement; its omission is a ground for annulment (Art 263(2) TFEU). The CoR may itself sue to protect its prerogatives (Art 263(3)) and for breach of subsidiarity (Art 8 Protocol No 2).
Codex: Art 13 TEU; Art 263, 285–287, 300–307, 319 TFEU; Protocol No 2, Art 8.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: By a regulation based on Art 114 TFEU, the EU legislature creates a 'European Battery Safety Agency' in Vienna with power to adopt binding decisions banning dangerous batteries in emergencies. Member State Westland objects that the Treaties do not mention such an agency and that powers may not be delegated to it. (a) Distinguish decentralised and executive agencies. (b) Assess Westland's objections. (c) How can a manufacturer challenge a ban decision of the agency? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Decentralised agencies may be created by secondary law on the relevant policy legal basis (including Art 114 TFEU) and may receive clearly circumscribed powers (Meroni, ESMA); their acts are reviewable under Art 263 TFEU.
• (a) Decentralised (regulatory) agencies: created by a legislative act, own legal personality, independent, run by a management board (e.g. EMA, EFSA, EASA, Frontex, the Fundamental Rights Agency in Vienna). Executive agencies: set up by the Commission for a limited period under Council Regulation 58/2003 to manage Union programmes – an extension of the Commission.
• (b) No express Treaty basis is needed: the legislature may create a body contributing to harmonisation under Art 114 TFEU (UK v Parliament and Council, C-217/04 ENISA). Delegation: under Meroni (9/56) only clearly defined executive powers may be delegated, not a wide discretion; the Court held that ESMA's intervention powers were compatible because they were circumscribed by precise criteria and subject to review (UK v Parliament and Council, C-270/12, 2014). If the battery agency's powers are similarly delimited, Westland's objections fail.
• (c) Action for annulment: acts of bodies, offices or agencies intended to produce legal effects vis-à-vis third parties are reviewable (Art 263(1) TFEU); the founding act may prescribe prior internal appeal (Art 263(5)); the manufacturer as addressee has standing (Art 263(4)), time limit two months (Art 263(6)), before the General Court (Art 256(1)).
Codex: Art 114, 256, 263, 267, 277 TFEU · Meroni (9/56), ESMA (C-270/12), ENISA (C-217/04).

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: Why is the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy said to wear a 'double hat'? How is he or she appointed? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The High Representative chairs the Foreign Affairs Council and is at the same time a Vice-President of the Commission (Art 18 TEU); appointed by the European Council by QMV with the agreement of the Commission President.
• Appointment (Art 18(1) TEU): European Council by QMV with the Commission President's agreement (same procedure to end the term); as a Commissioner also subject to the EP's consent vote on the college (Art 17(7)).
• Council hat: conducts the CFSP as mandated by the Council (Art 18(2)) and chairs the Foreign Affairs Council (Art 18(3)).
• Commission hat: Vice-President responsible for external relations (Art 18(4)); resigns if the President requests (Art 17(6)) and, after censure, from Commission duties (Art 17(8)). Supported by the EEAS (Art 27(3)).
Codex: Art 17(6)–(8), 18, 27(3) TEU.

cards.q: To improve student mobility, the Commission proposes a directive harmonising the mathematics curricula of all national secondary schools, based on Art 165 TFEU; as a fallback it suggests Art 352 TFEU. Does the Union have the competence to adopt such a directive? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – education is only a supporting competence in which harmonisation is excluded (Art 2(5), 6(e), 165(4) TFEU), and Art 352(3) TFEU cannot be used to circumvent that exclusion.
• Principle of conferral: the Union acts only within the limits of the competences conferred on it by the Member States in the Treaties; competences not conferred remain with the Member States (Art 4(1), 5(1)–(2) TEU); institutions act within their powers (Art 13(2) TEU).
• Category: education, vocational training, youth and sport are areas where the Union may only support, coordinate or supplement Member State action (Art 2(5), 6(e) TFEU); binding acts there 'shall not entail harmonisation of Member States' laws or regulations'.
• Legal basis: Art 165(1) TFEU requires full respect for the Member States' responsibility for the content of teaching and the organisation of education systems; Art 165(4) allows only incentive measures 'excluding any harmonisation' and Council recommendations.
• Art 352 TFEU: measures based on it 'shall not entail harmonisation … in cases where the Treaties exclude such harmonisation' (Art 352(3)). Nor could Art 114 TFEU be used to circumvent an express exclusion (Tobacco Advertising, C-376/98).
• Consequence: the directive would be adopted without competence and could be annulled (Art 263(2) TFEU – lack of competence). Admissible alternatives: Erasmus-type incentive programmes or a Council recommendation.
Codex: Art 4(1), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU; Art 2(5), 6(e), 165, 352 TFEU · Tobacco Advertising (C-376/98).

cards.q: Name the categories of Union competences, their legal consequences and give two examples of each. Why can an act never be based on Art 3 TFEU itself? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Exclusive, shared, coordinating (economic/employment), CFSP and supporting competences (Art 2–6 TFEU); the catalogue only defines the type – the legal basis is in the policy chapters (Art 2(6) TFEU).
• Exclusive (Art 2(1), 3 TFEU): only the Union legislates; Member States only if empowered or to implement Union acts. Areas (Art 3(1)): customs union, competition rules necessary for the internal market, monetary policy for the euro area, conservation of marine biological resources under the common fisheries policy, common commercial policy; plus international agreements in the cases of Art 3(2) (codified ERTA).
• Shared (Art 2(2), 4 TFEU): both may legislate; Member States only to the extent the Union has not exercised (or has ceased to exercise) its competence – pre-emption. E.g. internal market, environment, consumer protection, transport, energy, AFSJ, social policy (aspects defined), agriculture. No pre-emption in research/space and development cooperation/humanitarian aid (Art 4(3)–(4)).
• Coordination of economic and employment policies (Art 2(3), 5 TFEU): Member States coordinate within arrangements laid down by the Union (broad economic policy guidelines, Art 121).
• CFSP (Art 2(4) TFEU; Art 24 et seq. TEU): specific rules, mostly unanimity, no legislative acts (Art 24(1), 31(1) TEU).
• Supporting/coordinating/supplementing (Art 2(5), 6 TFEU): no supersession of national competence and no harmonisation – e.g. human health, industry, culture, tourism, education, civil protection.
• Art 2(6) TFEU: scope and arrangements are determined by the provisions relating to each area – so a directive on competition is based on Art 103 TFEU, not on Art 3(1)(b).
Codex: Art 4(1), 5 TEU; Art 2–6, 103 TFEU; Art 24 TEU.

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statements? Give reasons. (a) 'Austria may unilaterally lower its customs duties on solar panels imported from China to help the energy transition.' (b) 'Before acting in an area of exclusive competence, the Union must show that the Member States could not achieve the objective sufficiently.' (c) 'In areas of exclusive competence, Member States may never adopt legally binding acts.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) false, (b) false, (c) false.
• (a) False. The customs union and the common commercial policy are exclusive Union competences (Art 3(1)(a) and (e) TFEU). Common Customs Tariff duties are fixed by the Council on a Commission proposal (Art 31 TFEU); customs duties between Member States and on third-country goods are not a national matter. Austria could act only if empowered by the Union (Art 2(1) TFEU).
• (b) False. The subsidiarity principle applies only 'in areas which do not fall within its exclusive competence' (Art 5(3) TEU). In exclusive areas only proportionality applies (Art 5(4) TEU).
• (c) False. Art 2(1) TFEU allows Member States to legislate and adopt binding acts in exclusive areas 'if so empowered by the Union or for the implementation of Union acts' – e.g. specific authorisations in commercial policy, or national measures for the conservation of fish stocks acting as 'trustees of the common interest' where the Union has not acted (Commission v UK, 804/79).
Codex: Art 5(3)–(4) TEU; Art 2(1), 3(1), 31 TFEU.

cards.q: The Union adopts a directive on packaging waste under Art 192(1) TFEU, requiring 65% of packaging to be recycled. Austria wants to prescribe 75%. (a) May it do so? (b) Would the answer differ if the directive were a full harmonisation measure adopted under Art 114 TFEU? (c) May Austria also run its own space research programme parallel to the Union's programme? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) yes, under the environmental minimum-harmonisation clause (Art 193 TFEU); (b) in principle no, only via Art 114(4)–(5) TFEU; (c) yes, research and space are shared competences without pre-emption (Art 4(3) TFEU).
• Pre-emption (Art 2(2) TFEU): in shared areas Member States exercise their competence only to the extent that the Union has not exercised its competence; they regain it where the Union ceases to act. Pre-emption covers only the elements governed by the Union act, not the whole area (Protocol No 25).
• (a) Environment is a shared competence (Art 4(2)(e) TFEU). Art 193 TFEU: protective measures adopted under Art 192 'shall not prevent any Member State from maintaining or introducing more stringent protective measures', which must be compatible with the Treaties (e.g. free movement of goods, Art 34–36 TFEU) and be notified to the Commission. So 75% is allowed.
• (b) An exhaustive (full) harmonisation of the internal market occupies the field: stricter national rules are excluded unless the directive itself allows them or the derogation procedure of Art 114(4)–(6) TFEU is followed (notification and Commission approval).
• (c) Art 4(3) TFEU: in research, technological development and space the Union may define and implement programmes, but 'the exercise of that competence shall not result in Member States being prevented from exercising theirs' (same for development cooperation and humanitarian aid, Art 4(4)).
Codex: Art 2(2), 4(2)–(4), 114, 192, 193 TFEU; Protocol No 25 on the exercise of shared competence.

cards.q: Explain the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. Where are they regulated, when do they apply, and how is compliance controlled? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both govern the exercise (not the existence) of Union competences – subsidiarity (Art 5(3) TEU) only in non-exclusive areas, proportionality (Art 5(4) TEU) for all Union action – and are policed by national parliaments under Protocol No 2 and by the CJEU.
• Subsidiarity, Art 5(3) TEU: in areas not within its exclusive competence the Union acts only if and in so far as the objectives cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States, either at central or at regional and local level (negative criterion), but can rather, by reason of the scale or effects of the proposed action, be better achieved at Union level (positive criterion, 'added value').
• Proportionality, Art 5(4) TEU: the content and form of Union action shall not exceed what is necessary to achieve the objectives of the Treaties – suitable, necessary (least restrictive means), not manifestly inappropriate; the legislature has broad discretion, review is limited to manifest error (Fedesa, C-331/88; Vodafone, C-58/08).
• Control: institutions apply both under Protocol No 2 and must justify draft legislative acts in a detailed statement (Art 5 Protocol 2; Art 296(2) TFEU); national parliaments' early-warning mechanism – reasoned opinions within eight weeks, yellow and orange cards (Art 6–7 Protocol 2; Art 12(b) TEU); ex post: action for annulment by a Member State on behalf of its national parliament or by the Committee of the Regions (Art 8 Protocol 2, Art 263 TFEU). Court review is marginal (Germany v EP and Council, C-233/94; Alliance for Natural Health, C-154/04).
Codex: Art 5(3)–(4), 12(b) TEU; Art 263, 296 TFEU; Protocols No 1 and 2 · Fedesa, Vodafone, C-233/94.

cards.q: The Commission submits a proposal for a regulation under the ordinary legislative procedure. Within the deadline, national parliaments holding 20 of the 54 votes send reasoned opinions stating that the proposal breaches subsidiarity. (a) What is the consequence? (b) What would change if they held 28 votes? (c) Which threshold would apply to a draft under Art 76 TFEU in police cooperation? (d) The regulation is adopted anyway. What can the Austrian Bundesrat do? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: 20 votes trigger a yellow card (review), 28 an orange card (review plus possible stop by the legislators); for Art 76 TFEU drafts a quarter suffices; after adoption an annulment action under Art 8 Protocol No 2 is possible.
• Procedure: each national parliament may send a reasoned opinion within eight weeks of transmission of the draft (Art 6 Protocol No 2); each parliament has two votes, one per chamber in bicameral systems (Art 7(1)) – 27 states = 54 votes; Austria: Nationalrat and Bundesrat one vote each.
• (a) Yellow card: opinions representing at least one third of the votes (18 of 54) – 20 is enough. The draft must be reviewed; the Commission may maintain, amend or withdraw it, giving reasons (Art 7(2)). No binding veto (used e.g. Monti II 2012 – withdrawn; EPPO 2013 – maintained).
• (b) Orange card (only in the OLP): at least a simple majority of the votes (28 of 54). If the Commission maintains the proposal it must justify this in a reasoned opinion; before the end of the first reading the legislators consider it, and if 55% of the Council members or a majority of the votes cast in the EP find a breach of subsidiarity, the proposal is not given further consideration (Art 7(3)).
• (c) One quarter of the votes (14 of 54) for drafts under Art 76 TFEU (Art 7(2) second sentence).
• (d) Under Art 8 Protocol No 2 the Court has jurisdiction in annulment actions (Art 263 TFEU) for infringement of subsidiarity brought by Member States or notified by them on behalf of a national parliament or a chamber – Austria must bring the action on the Bundesrat's behalf (Art 23h B-VG); two-month time limit (Art 263(6)). The Committee of the Regions may also sue where it had to be consulted.
Codex: Art 5(3), 12(b) TEU; Art 76, 263 TFEU; Protocol No 2, Art 6, 7, 8.

cards.q: The Commission wants to create a new supranational legal form, the 'European Foundation', which would exist alongside national foundations. No Treaty article expressly provides for this. (a) Can the Union act, and on which basis? (b) Describe the procedure and limits. (c) Could the same article be used to accede to a new international human-rights treaty with far-reaching institutional consequences? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, under the flexibility clause Art 352 TFEU (Council unanimity, EP consent), within its limits; it cannot be used for changes of constitutional significance.
• (a) Art 114 TFEU is unsuitable because a new legal form existing alongside national forms does not approximate national laws (EP v Council, C-436/03, European Cooperative Society – Art 308 EC, now Art 352, was the correct basis). Art 352(1) TFEU: if action by the Union proves necessary, within the framework of the policies defined in the Treaties, to attain one of the Treaties' objectives, and the Treaties have not provided the necessary powers.
• (b) Council acting unanimously on a Commission proposal after obtaining the EP's consent (Art 352(1)); the Commission draws national parliaments' attention to the proposal under the subsidiarity procedure (Art 352(2)); no harmonisation where the Treaties exclude it (Art 352(3)); no use for CFSP objectives (Art 352(4)); Declarations No 41 and 42: it cannot serve to widen Union powers beyond the general framework of the Treaties or be a substitute for Treaty amendment. Nationally, e.g. the German representative may only vote after a German statute (BVerfG Lisbon judgment 2009).
• (c) No. Changes of constitutional significance require a Treaty amendment – accession to the ECHR could not be based on the former Art 235 EC (Opinion 2/94); hence Art 6(2) TEU was introduced.
Codex: Art 352, 114 TFEU; Art 6(2), 48 TEU; Declarations No 41 and 42 · C-436/03, Opinion 2/94.

cards.q: The Union legislator wants to adopt a directive harmonising the framework under which national competition authorities enforce Union and national competition law – guarantees on their independence, resources and powers – while ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market and of the European Competition Network. What is the proper legal basis for this directive, and which procedure follows from it? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 103 TFEU (giving effect to Arts 101 and 102) combined with Art 114 TFEU (internal market harmonisation) – the actual ECN+ Directive (EU) 2019/1 rests on both and was adopted by the EP and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure.
• Two steps: (1) Catalogue: competition rules necessary for the functioning of the internal market are an exclusive competence (Art 3(1)(b) TFEU); the internal market is shared (Art 4(2)(a)). (2) Legal basis from the policy chapter (Art 2(6) TFEU).
• Art 103(1) TFEU: the Council, on a Commission proposal and after consulting the EP, lays down regulations or directives to give effect to the principles of Arts 101 and 102 – in particular to define the relationship between national laws and the competition provisions (Art 103(2)(e)). This covers the effective application of Arts 101/102 by national authorities (as Regulation 1/2003).
• Art 114 TFEU (OLP after consulting the EESC): approximation of national provisions with the object of establishing and functioning of the internal market – the directive also harmonises national procedural and institutional law for enforcing national competition law and removes distortions caused by differing enforcement.
• Choice: based on objective factors – aim and content (Titanium dioxide, C-300/89); where a measure pursues two inseparable objectives neither of which is secondary, a dual legal basis is used, provided the procedures are compatible and the EP's rights are not undermined – here the co-decision (OLP) was applied.
• Wrong answer to avoid: 'Art 3(1)(b) TFEU' – the catalogue is never a legal basis.
Codex: Art 2(6), 3(1)(b), 4(2)(a), 101–103, 114, 294 TFEU · Titanium dioxide (C-300/89).

cards.q: Based on Art 114 TFEU, the EU adopts a directive banning all advertising of tobacco products – including posters, ashtrays in cafés and cinema adverts – whose recitals mainly stress the protection of public health.
