Germany brings an action for annulment. (a) How is the correct legal basis determined? (b) Will Germany succeed? (c) What is the consequence of a wrong legal basis? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The legal basis follows the aim and content of the measure (centre of gravity); Art 114 TFEU does not cover a general ban aimed at health, so the action succeeds (Tobacco Advertising I, C-376/98).
• (a) The choice of legal basis must rest on objective factors amenable to judicial review, in particular the aim and content of the measure (Titanium dioxide, C-300/89). If a measure pursues several aims, the predominant one ('centre of gravity') decides; only if the aims are inseparable and equal is a dual basis used, provided the procedures are compatible.
• (b) Art 114 TFEU requires a measure that genuinely improves the conditions for the establishment and functioning of the internal market – eliminating obstacles to free movement or appreciable distortions of competition; a mere finding of disparities or an abstract risk is not enough, and Art 114 confers no general power to regulate the internal market (C-376/98, 2000). Posters, ashtrays and cinema adverts involve hardly any cross-border trade; the real aim is public health, where harmonisation is excluded (Art 168(5) TFEU). Art 114(3) (high level of health protection) cannot be used to circumvent this. → Annulled. A narrower directive on cross-border media (press, radio, internet) was later upheld (Tobacco Advertising II, C-380/03).
• (c) A wrong legal basis is a ground for annulment (lack of competence / infringement of the Treaties or of essential procedural requirements, Art 263(2) TFEU), unless the error is purely formal and did not affect the procedure or content.
Codex: Art 5(2) TEU; Art 114, 168(5), 263 TFEU · Titanium dioxide (C-300/89), Tobacco Advertising I (C-376/98) and II (C-380/03).

cards.q: Based on Art 114 TFEU, a directive harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances. Years later, a study published in Spain concludes that the maximum concentration of the chemical 'PCP' allowed under the directive may be too high. Spain wants to adopt new, stricter rules deviating from the harmonised standard. (a) Under what conditions is this permitted? (2 points) The Commission considers the Spanish 'solo action' unjustified and wants to bring an infringement action. (b) Must it conduct a pre-litigation procedure? (1 point) (c) Must it prove its own legal interest? (1 point) (d) What legal effect does a judgment establishing the infringement have? (1 point) (e) Is an appeal against the judgment possible? (1 point) (6 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: New stricter national rules are permitted only under Art 114(5)–(6) TFEU (new scientific evidence, environment or working environment, specific problem, notification and Commission approval); the Commission may go directly to the Court (Art 114(9)), needs no legal interest, obtains a declaratory judgment, and there is no appeal.
• (a) Art 114(5): to INTRODUCE new provisions after harmonisation, Spain needs (1) new scientific evidence, (2) relating to the protection of the environment or the working environment, (3) on grounds of a problem specific to Spain, (4) arising after the adoption of the measure; it must notify the envisaged provisions and grounds to the Commission. (Art 114(4) – Art 36 grounds or environment – concerns only MAINTAINING existing national provisions; a pure public-health problem only leads to Art 114(8).) Art 114(6): the Commission approves or rejects within six months after checking arbitrary discrimination, disguised restriction on trade and obstacles to the internal market; silence = deemed approval; extension up to six more months. Spain may not apply the rules before approval; it bears the burden of proof (Land Oberösterreich and Austria v Commission, C-439/05 P – Upper Austrian GMO ban rejected). A general study on PCP's toxicity hardly shows a problem specific to Spain.
• (b) No. By derogation from Arts 258 and 259, the Commission (or any Member State) may bring the matter directly before the CJEU if it considers that a state is making improper use of the powers under Art 114 (Art 114(9)) – no letter of formal notice or reasoned opinion. It may also choose the ordinary Art 258 route with pre-litigation.
• (c) No. The infringement procedure is objective; as guardian of the Treaties (Art 17(1) TEU) the Commission need not show a specific interest and has discretion whether to sue.
• (d) Declaratory: the Court finds the failure; Spain must take the necessary measures to comply (Art 260(1)); the national law is not annulled. If Spain does not comply, the Commission may bring a second action and the COURT (not the Commission) may impose a lump sum or penalty payment (Art 260(2)).
• (e) No. Infringement actions are decided by the Court of Justice at first and last instance. Spain's remedy was to challenge the Commission's rejection decision (Art 263 TFEU, two months).
Codex: Art 114(4)–(9), 258, 260, 263 TFEU; Art 17(1) TEU · Land Oberösterreich (C-439/05 P).

cards.q: Explain the individual steps of the ordinary legislative procedure, including the majorities and time limits. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 289(1) and 294 TFEU: Commission proposal → first reading (no time limit) → second reading (3 months + 3 months) → conciliation (6 weeks) → third reading (6 weeks); the act needs the agreement of both EP and Council.
• Proposal: the Commission submits a proposal to the EP and the Council (Art 294(2)); the Council can amend it only unanimously (Art 293(1)); the Commission may alter or withdraw it as long as the Council has not acted (Art 293(2)). National parliaments get the draft (Protocols No 1 and 2).
• First reading: the EP adopts its position (simple majority of votes cast) and communicates it to the Council (294(3)). If the Council approves it (QMV), the act is adopted in that wording (294(4)); otherwise the Council adopts its own first-reading position and communicates it with reasons (294(5)–(6)). No time limit.
• Second reading (EP, within three months, 294(7)): (a) approves the Council position or takes no decision → act adopted; (b) rejects it by a majority of its component members → not adopted; (c) proposes amendments by a majority of its component members → text to Council and Commission (Commission opinion). Council within three months (294(8)): approves all amendments (QMV; unanimity for amendments with a negative Commission opinion, 294(9)) → adopted; otherwise the Council President, with the EP President, convenes the Conciliation Committee within six weeks.
• Conciliation (294(10)–(12)): equal numbers of Council members (27) and MEPs, with the Commission; joint text within six weeks, by QMV of the Council side and a majority of the EP delegation; no joint text → not adopted.
• Third reading (294(13)): within six weeks, EP (majority of votes cast) and Council (QMV) each approve the joint text, otherwise not adopted.
• Extensions: three months by one month, six weeks by two weeks (294(14)). Then signature by both Presidents and publication in the OJ (Art 297(1)).
Codex: Art 289(1), 293, 294, 297 TFEU; Art 16(3), 17(2) TEU.

cards.q: The ordinary legislative procedure involves the joint adoption of an act by the Council and the European Parliament on a Commission proposal. (a) Name one document the Commission issues in the preparatory, strategic-planning phase of a legislative proposal. (b) What control mechanism do national parliaments have if they believe the objectives of a proposed regulation can be sufficiently achieved at Member State level? (c) Where is the ordinary legislative procedure regulated? (d) Must an act always go through three readings? (e) What happens if the Council, in second reading, does not approve all of Parliament's amendments? (f) When do acts adopted under the OLP enter into force? (6 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) e.g. the Commission Work Programme or a Green/White Paper; (b) the subsidiarity early-warning mechanism of Protocol No 2; (c) Art 289(1), 294 TFEU; (d) no; (e) conciliation; (f) on the date specified or on the 20th day after publication (Art 297(1) TFEU).
• (a) Annual Commission Work Programme (programming, Art 17(1) TEU), Green Papers (consultation), White Papers (concrete proposals for action), impact assessments and calls for evidence under Better Regulation. The proposal itself is the result, not a planning document.
• (b) Reasoned opinions within eight weeks claiming breach of subsidiarity (Art 5(3) TEU, Art 12(b) TEU; Art 6–7 Protocol No 2): yellow card (1/3 of votes) → review; orange card (simple majority, OLP only) → review and possible stop by EP or Council; afterwards annulment action under Art 8 Protocol No 2.
• (c) Art 289(1) TFEU (definition) and Art 294 TFEU (steps); Art 293 TFEU on amending the proposal.
• (d) No. The act is adopted at first reading if the Council approves the EP's first-reading position (Art 294(4)) – today about 89% of files, prepared by informal trilogues; at second reading if the EP approves the Council's position or does not act within three months (294(7)(a)) or the Council approves all EP amendments (294(8)(a)).
• (e) The President of the Council, in agreement with the EP President, convenes the Conciliation Committee within six weeks (294(8)(b)); it seeks a joint text within six weeks (294(10)); if agreed, EP and Council adopt it in third reading within six weeks (294(13)); otherwise the act fails (294(12)).
• (f) Signed by the Presidents of the EP and the Council and published in the Official Journal; enters into force on the date specified in it or, failing that, on the twentieth day following publication (Art 297(1) TFEU). Entry into force is distinct from the date of application or a transposition deadline.
Codex: Art 5(3), 12(b), 17(1) TEU; Art 289, 293, 294, 297 TFEU; Protocols No 1 and 2.

cards.q: In the ordinary legislative procedure the Council communicates its first-reading position to the European Parliament (720 members) on 1 March. (a) On 20 May, 550 MEPs vote on amendments: 350 in favour, 200 against; a motion to reject finds no majority either. What is the result? (b) Alternatively, the EP adopts amendments by 380 votes; the Commission gives a negative opinion on two of them; the Council approves all other amendments by QMV, but on the two contested ones only 24 states vote in favour. What follows? (c) The Conciliation Committee reaches no joint text within six weeks. Result? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) The act is deemed adopted in the Council's wording; (b) conciliation must be convened; (c) the act is not adopted.
• (a) Second reading, Art 294(7) TFEU: amendments and rejection require a majority of the EP's component members, i.e. 361 of 720 – 350 votes are not enough, however many were cast. If within three months (here by 1 June, extendable by one month, Art 294(14)) the EP neither approves nor validly rejects or amends, it 'has not taken a decision' and the act is deemed adopted in the wording of the Council's position (294(7)(a)).
• (b) 380 ≥ 361 → amendments validly adopted (294(7)(c)). Council second reading: QMV for amendments, but UNANIMITY for amendments on which the Commission has delivered a negative opinion (294(9)); 24 of 27 is not unanimity → the Council has not approved all amendments → the Council President, in agreement with the EP President, convenes the Conciliation Committee within six weeks (294(8)(b)).
• (c) The Committee (27 Council members or representatives and 27 MEPs; the Commission participates) must approve a joint text within six weeks by QMV of the Council side and a majority of the EP side (294(10)–(11)). Without a joint text the proposed act is deemed not to have been adopted (294(12)). Only an approved joint text goes to the third reading (EP majority of votes cast, Council QMV, six weeks, 294(13)).
Codex: Art 294(7)–(14) TFEU; Art 14(2) TEU (720 MEPs).

cards.q: (a) How does the ordinary legislative procedure (Art 289(1), 294 TFEU) differ from the special legislative procedure (Art 289(2) TFEU)? (b) What are acts adopted under Art 289 TFEU called? (c) The Council adopts a directive combating discrimination on grounds of religion under Art 19(1) TFEU after merely consulting the Parliament. Is it valid? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) In the OLP EP and Council decide jointly as equal co-legislators; in a special procedure one of them adopts the act with the mere participation (consent or consultation) of the other; (b) legislative acts; (c) no – Art 19(1) requires the EP's consent.
• (a) OLP: joint adoption of a regulation, directive or decision by EP and Council on a Commission proposal following the stages of Art 294 (Art 289(1)). Special legislative procedure: in specific cases provided by the Treaties, adoption by the Council with the participation of the EP (usually unanimity, e.g. Art 113 tax harmonisation – consultation; Art 312(2) MFF – consent) or by the EP with the participation of the Council (e.g. Art 223(2), 226, 228(4)) (Art 289(2)). Consent = yes/no veto without amendments; consultation = opinion must be awaited but does not bind (failure to consult annuls the act, Roquette Frères, 138/79; re-consultation if the text changes substantially).
• (b) 'Legislative acts' (Art 289(3)) – the label depends on the procedure, not the form. Consequences: public Council deliberation (Art 16(8) TEU), subsidiarity scrutiny (Protocol No 2), power to delegate (Art 290), and they are not 'regulatory acts' under Art 263(4) (Inuit, C-583/11 P).
• (c) Art 19(1) TFEU: the Council acts unanimously in accordance with a special legislative procedure 'after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament'. Consultation instead of consent infringes an essential procedural requirement and the EP's prerogatives → annulment (Art 263(2) TFEU; the EP may sue as privileged applicant).
Codex: Art 16(8) TEU; Art 19, 113, 263, 289, 290, 294, 312 TFEU · Roquette Frères (138/79), Inuit (C-583/11 P).

cards.q: For three years the Council has failed to agree unanimously on a directive creating a common framework for taxing digital services. Eight Member States now want to go ahead alone through 'enhanced cooperation'; later a ninth joins them. Spain objects that this would fragment the internal market. (a) What is enhanced cooperation and what are its conditions? (b) Can the eight proceed? (c) Describe the authorisation procedure. (d) Assess Spain's objection. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Enhanced cooperation (Art 20 TEU, Art 326–334 TFEU) allows at least nine Member States to use the EU institutions in non-exclusive areas as a last resort; eight are not enough, nine are.
• (a) Conditions (Art 20 TEU): only within non-exclusive competences; aims to further the Union's objectives and reinforce integration; open at any time to all Member States (Art 328 TFEU); authorised only as a LAST RESORT, when the Council has established that the objectives cannot be attained within a reasonable period by the Union as a whole (Art 20(2)); at least NINE Member States. It must comply with the Treaties and Union law, not undermine the internal market or cohesion, not constitute a barrier to trade or distort competition (Art 326 TFEU) and respect non-participants' rights (Art 327).
• (b) Tax harmonisation (Art 113 TFEU) is a non-exclusive area, and three years of failed negotiations can show last resort – but eight states are below the threshold; with nine participants the request is possible.
• (c) Request to the Commission specifying scope and objectives; the Commission may submit a proposal (or explains why not); authorisation by the Council (all members vote, QMV) after obtaining the EP's consent (Art 329(1) TFEU); in the CFSP: request to the Council, unanimous decision (Art 329(2)). Afterwards only participating states vote on the acts (Art 20(3) TEU; Art 330 TFEU with Art 238(3)); the acts bind only them and are not acquis for candidates (Art 20(4) TEU).
• (d) The Court reviews whether the conditions are met but accepts the Council's assessment of last resort if negotiations were genuinely deadlocked; enhanced cooperation does not per se undermine the internal market (Spain and Italy v Council, C-274/11 and C-295/11, unitary patent). Spain may join later (Art 331). Examples: Rome III divorce regulation (2010), unitary patent (2012), property regimes (2016), EPPO (2017).
Codex: Art 20 TEU; Art 113, 326–334, 238(3) TFEU · C-274/11 and C-295/11.

cards.q: The European Council wants the Council to adopt CFSP sanctions and certain tax measures by qualified majority instead of unanimity, without a Treaty amendment ratified by all Member States. Is that possible, and how? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, through a passerelle clause – general (Art 48(7) TEU) or specific (e.g. Art 31(3) TEU for the CFSP) – but not for military or defence matters.
• General passerelle, Art 48(7) TEU: where the TFEU or Title V TEU requires Council unanimity, the European Council may authorise QMV (first subpara; not for decisions with military or defence implications); where the TFEU provides for a special legislative procedure, it may authorise the OLP (second subpara). Conditions: the initiative is notified to national parliaments; if one national parliament objects within six months, the decision is not adopted; the European Council acts unanimously after obtaining the EP's consent by a majority of its component members.
• Specific passerelles: Art 31(3) TEU (CFSP: unanimous European Council decision; excluded for military/defence, Art 31(4)); Art 81(3), 153(2), 192(2), 312(2), 333 TFEU.
• Distinguish the simplified revision procedure Art 48(6) TEU (amending Part III TFEU; approval by all states under their constitutional requirements; cannot increase Union competences – used for Art 136(3) TFEU, Pringle C-370/12).
Codex: Art 31(3)–(4), 48(6)–(7) TEU; Art 333 TFEU.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'The Charter of Fundamental Rights ranks below the Treaties because it was only solemnly proclaimed.' (b) 'Protocols and declarations annexed to the Treaties are both mere political statements without legal force.' (c) 'The TFEU ranks above the TEU because it contains the detailed rules.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false – the Charter, protocols, TEU and TFEU all belong to primary law with equal rank; only declarations are non-binding.
• (a) False. Although first proclaimed at Nice (2000), since the Treaty of Lisbon the Charter has 'the same legal value as the Treaties' (Art 6(1) TEU) and is thus primary law; it binds the institutions and the Member States when implementing Union law (Art 51(1) Charter).
• (b) Partly false. Protocols and annexes 'form an integral part' of the Treaties (Art 51 TEU) and have the same legal force (e.g. Protocol No 2 on subsidiarity). Declarations annexed to the Final Act (e.g. Declaration 17 on primacy) are not legally binding; they only serve as aids to interpretation.
• (c) False. The TEU and TFEU 'have the same legal value' (Art 1(3) TEU, Art 1(2) TFEU); within primary law there is no hierarchy – conflicts are resolved by lex specialis and lex posterior. Primary law also comprises accession treaties and the general principles of law (Art 6(3) TEU). Amendment only through Art 48 TEU.
Codex: Art 1(3), 6, 48, 51 TEU; Art 1(2) TFEU; Art 51 Charter · Declaration 17.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: An EU regulation adopted in 2026 retroactively imposes, from 2024, a levy on importers who had relied on earlier assurances by the Commission that no levy would be charged. No Treaty article or Charter provision expressly prohibits retroactivity. (a) What are general principles of EU law, where do they come from, and what functions do they serve? (b) Can the importers invoke them here? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: General principles are unwritten primary law derived by the CJEU from the Treaties' system and the common constitutional traditions; legal certainty and legitimate expectations can render the retroactive levy invalid.
• (a) Sources: the telos and system of the Treaties and the constitutional traditions common to the Member States, confirmed and developed by the Court; recognised in Art 6(3) TEU (fundamental rights as general principles) and Art 340(2) TFEU. Examples: fundamental rights (Stauder, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft), proportionality (Art 5(4) TEU), legal certainty and protection of legitimate expectations, non-retroactivity, equal treatment and non-discrimination (e.g. age – Mangold, C-144/04), effective judicial protection (Johnston, 222/84; now Art 19(1) TEU, Art 47 Charter), right to be heard. Rank: primary law. Functions: filling gaps, interpreting EU and national implementing law, and a standard for reviewing the validity of Union acts and of Member State acts within the scope of EU law.
• (b) Legal certainty in principle precludes a measure from taking effect before its publication; exceptionally retroactivity is allowed where the purpose so demands and the legitimate expectations of those concerned are duly respected (Racke, 98/78). Here the importers relied on specific Commission assurances → the retroactive levy likely infringes legitimate expectations. Remedy: action for annulment (Art 263(4), 263(6) TFEU – two months), or plea in national proceedings leading to a preliminary reference on validity (Art 267; only the CJEU can declare invalidity – Foto-Frost, 314/85).
Codex: Art 5(4), 6(3), 19(1) TEU; Art 263, 267, 340(2) TFEU; Art 47 Charter · Racke (98/78), Mangold, Foto-Frost.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: The EU concluded a trade agreement with Andoria reducing customs duties on steel. (a) A later EU regulation raises those duties again contrary to the agreement. (b) The agreement also sets up a dispute body whose rulings would bind the Union's institutions on the interpretation of EU law. Where do international agreements rank in the EU legal order, and what follows in (a) and (b)? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: International agreements rank below primary law but above secondary law (Art 216(2) TFEU) – so the regulation may be reviewed against the agreement, while the agreement itself must respect the Treaties and the autonomy of EU law.
• Binding force: agreements concluded by the Union are binding upon the institutions and the Member States (Art 216(2) TFEU) and form an integral part of EU law from their entry into force (Haegeman, 181/73).
• (a) Primacy over secondary law: secondary law must be interpreted in conformity with the agreement and its validity can be reviewed against it (Commission v Germany, C-61/94; Intertanko, C-308/06), provided the nature and broad logic of the agreement do not preclude this and its provisions are unconditional and sufficiently precise. A bilateral tariff commitment usually qualifies → the regulation is invalid/annullable. (Exception: WTO law is generally not a standard of review – Portugal v Council, C-149/96.)
• (b) Rank below primary law: an agreement cannot affect the constitutional principles of the Treaties, including fundamental rights (Kadi, C-402/05 P) and the autonomy of EU law and the CJEU's exclusive jurisdiction (Opinion 2/13 on ECHR accession; Achmea, C-284/16). A Member State, the EP, the Council or the Commission may request an opinion before conclusion; if the opinion is adverse, the agreement may not enter into force unless amended or the Treaties are revised (Art 218(11) TFEU).
Codex: Art 216(2), 218(11), 263, 267 TFEU · Haegeman, Intertanko, Kadi, Opinion 2/13.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: Which legal instrument of Art 288 TFEU should be used, and why, if the Union wants (a) to lay down identical roaming-charge rules applying immediately to all operators in all Member States, (b) to oblige Member States to guarantee a minimum paid annual leave while leaving them the choice of how to implement it, (c) to fine a specific company for a cartel, (d) to encourage Member States to raise vaccination rates without any obligation? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) regulation, (b) directive, (c) decision, (d) recommendation.
• (a) Regulation, Art 288(2): general application, binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States – no national transposition needed, uniform rules immediately.
• (b) Directive, Art 288(3): binding as to the result to be achieved upon each Member State to which it is addressed, but leaves the choice of form and methods to the national authorities – requires transposition by a deadline.
• (c) Decision, Art 288(4): binding in its entirety; where it specifies addressees, binding only on them – the instrument for individual cases (e.g. Commission competition decision under Regulation 1/2003, Art 105 TFEU); takes effect on notification (Art 297(2) TFEU).
• (d) Recommendation (or opinion), Art 288(5): no binding force – soft law (Council recommendations, Art 292 TFEU; health is only a supporting competence, Art 6(a), 168 TFEU).
• Where the Treaties do not prescribe the type of act, the institution chooses it case by case, respecting the procedures and proportionality (Art 296(1) TFEU); all binding acts must state reasons (Art 296(2)).
Codex: Art 288, 292, 296, 297 TFEU.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: A new EU regulation on food labelling applies from 1 March. Austria re-enacts its provisions word for word in the Austrian Food Act and provides that they apply from 1 May. Can a regulation nevertheless be transposed into national law? Assess Austria's approach. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: As a rule no – a regulation is directly applicable (Art 288(2) TFEU), and national re-enactment and a later date of application infringe EU law (Variola, 34/73).
• Direct applicability: a regulation enters into force and applies in all Member States independently of any national measure of reception (Art 288(2) TFEU; Art 297 TFEU publication).
• Prohibition of transposition: Member States must not adopt measures that conceal the EU nature of a rule and its effects from those subject to it, since this endangers its uniform application and the CJEU's jurisdiction to interpret it under Art 267 TFEU (Variola, 34/73); they may not alter, delay or make its application conditional (Commission v Italy, 39/72).
• Exceptions: (1) where the regulation itself requires or permits national implementing measures – designating authorities, laying down sanctions, using 'opening clauses' (e.g. GDPR); (2) limited repetition of regulation provisions is tolerated to keep a complex national regime coherent and comprehensible (Commission v Italy, 272/83; GDPR recital 8).
• Application: the word-for-word re-enactment is not needed; the postponement to 1 May breaches Art 288(2) and Art 4(3) TEU → infringement (Art 258 TFEU). Individuals may rely on the regulation from 1 March; the conflicting Austrian date must be disapplied (primacy, Simmenthal).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 258, 267, 288(2), 297 TFEU · Variola (34/73), Commission v Italy (39/72).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: An environmental directive had to be transposed by 31 December 2025. Austria considers its existing practice sufficient and in addition issues a ministerial circular to the provincial authorities telling them to apply the directive's limit values; the circular can be changed at any time and is not published. Has Austria fulfilled its obligations? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – a directive must be transposed by binding, sufficiently clear and published national provisions by the deadline; an internal circular or administrative practice is not enough.
• Art 288(3) TFEU: a directive binds each addressed Member State as to the result to be achieved and leaves the choice of form and methods; the Member State must take all appropriate measures (Art 4(3) TEU; Art 291(1) TFEU).
• Requirements from case law: transposition must be by provisions of binding force with the specificity, precision and clarity required by legal certainty, so that individuals can know their rights and obligations and invoke them in court; mere administrative practices, alterable at the administration's discretion and not publicised, are insufficient (Commission v Belgium, 102/79; Commission v Germany, C-59/89 TA Luft). An existing general legal context can suffice only if it actually guarantees full application in a clear and precise manner.
• Deadline: expired 31 Dec 2025 → failure to fulfil obligations; the Commission can bring an infringement action (Art 258 TFEU); for failure to notify transposition measures of a legislative directive the Court may impose a financial penalty already in the first judgment (Art 260(3)).
• Individuals: after the deadline they may rely on unconditional and sufficiently precise provisions against the state (vertical direct effect), national courts must interpret national law in conformity, and state liability may arise (Francovich).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 258, 260(3), 288(3), 291(1) TFEU · Commission v Belgium (102/79), TA Luft (C-59/89).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: (a) The Commission adopts a Recommendation on online gambling; Belgium wants to have it annulled. (b) A national labour court refuses to take a Commission recommendation on occupational diseases into account because it is 'not law'. (c) In a cartel case the Commission sets a fine far above what its own published Fining Guidelines would give, without explanation. Assess each situation. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Soft law is not binding, but it has indirect legal effects: (a) no annulment, (b) courts must take recommendations into consideration, (c) the Commission is self-bound by its guidelines.
• Soft law: instruments without binding force – recommendations and opinions (Art 288(5) TFEU), communications, guidelines, notices, Green and White Papers, codes of conduct.
• (a) Art 263(1) TFEU excludes recommendations and opinions from review; a recommendation is challengeable only if, in substance, it is intended to produce binding legal effects – not the case for the gambling recommendation (Belgium v Commission, C-16/16 P). By contrast, a 'communication' that in fact creates new obligations is annullable (France v Commission, C-325/91).
• (b) Wrong. Recommendations cannot create rights, but national courts are bound to take them into consideration when deciding disputes, in particular where they clarify the interpretation of national measures adopted to implement them or supplement binding EU measures (Grimaldi, C-322/88). They can also be interpreted by the CJEU under Art 267 TFEU.
• (c) By adopting guidelines the Commission limits its own discretion: it may not depart from them in an individual case without giving reasons compatible with equal treatment and legitimate expectations (Dansk Rørindustri, C-189/02 P) – the fine can be annulled or reduced (Art 263, 261 TFEU).
Codex: Art 261, 263(1), 267, 288(5), 292 TFEU · Grimaldi (C-322/88), C-16/16 P, Dansk Rørindustri (C-189/02 P).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: What is the difference between delegated acts and implementing acts? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Delegated acts (Art 290 TFEU) supplement or amend non-essential elements of a legislative act and are controlled by the EP and the Council; implementing acts (Art 291 TFEU) ensure uniform conditions for implementing binding Union acts and are controlled by the Member States through comitology.
• Delegated acts, Art 290: only a legislative act may delegate to the Commission the power to adopt non-legislative acts of general application supplementing or amending non-essential elements; objectives, content, scope and duration must be explicitly defined; essential elements are reserved (290(1)). Control: EP (majority of component members) or Council (QMV) may revoke the delegation or object, preventing entry into force (290(2)).
• Implementing acts, Art 291: implementation is primarily for the Member States (291(1)); where uniform conditions are needed, the basic act confers powers on the Commission, exceptionally on the Council (291(2)); control by the Member States under rules laid down in advance by EP and Council – Regulation 182/2011, advisory and examination procedures (291(3)).
• Delimitation: Art 290 = adding or changing norms; Art 291 = giving effect to/specifying the basic act without amending or supplementing it (Commission v EP and Council, C-88/14). The legislature has discretion to choose, reviewed only for manifest error (Biocides, C-427/12).
• Both are non-legislative, 'tertiary' law, ranking below the basic act.
Codex: Art 290, 291 TFEU; Art 24, 26 TEU · Regulation 182/2011 (not in codex) · Biocides (C-427/12), C-88/14.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: A regulation on maritime border surveillance (adopted under the OLP) empowers the Commission 'to adopt delegated acts supplementing the rules on sea operations'. The Commission adopts a delegated act authorising border guards to use force and to return intercepted persons to third countries. Three months later the European Parliament becomes concerned. (a) Could such rules be laid down in a delegated act? (b) What can the Parliament and the Council do, and until when? (c) What if the basic act had instead conferred implementing powers under Art 291 TFEU? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – rules on coercive powers and fundamental-rights interferences are essential elements reserved to the legislature (Art 290(1) TFEU; Parliament v Council, C-355/10); the EP can object/revoke or sue for annulment.
• (a) Art 290(1) second subpara TFEU: 'The essential elements of an area shall be reserved for the legislative act and accordingly shall not be the subject of a delegation of power.' Essential are elements requiring political choices falling within the responsibilities of the legislature and serious interferences with fundamental rights – conferring powers of force and return on border guards is essential (Parliament v Council, C-355/10, 2012, annulling a measure on the Schengen sea-surveillance rules for that reason). The delegated act exceeds the delegation.
• (b) Before entry into force: objection within the period set by the basic act (usually two months, extendable by two), by the EP (majority of component members) or the Council (QMV) → the act cannot enter into force (Art 290(2)(b)); revocation of the delegation for the future (Art 290(2)(a)). After three months the objection period has probably expired → action for annulment by the EP as privileged applicant, within two months of publication (Art 263(2), (6) TFEU), ground: infringement of the Treaties/basic act; the Court declares it void (Art 264). Any national court may also refer the question of validity (Art 267; Foto-Frost).
• (c) Implementing acts may not supplement or amend the basic act at all (C-88/14) – even more clearly unlawful. Control would be by comitology committees of Member State representatives (Regulation 182/2011); EP and Council only have a non-binding right of scrutiny (Art 11 of the regulation).
Codex: Art 290, 291, 263, 264, 267 TFEU · Parliament v Council (C-355/10), C-88/14, Foto-Frost (314/85).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: The Commission submits to a comitology committee, under the examination procedure, a draft implementing regulation renewing the approval of a controversial pesticide. (a) The committee reaches no qualified majority either for or against. May the Commission adopt the act? (b) What if the committee had delivered a negative opinion? (c) What if the basic act had prescribed the advisory procedure and the committee had voted against by simple majority? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Not directly – for acts protecting human, animal or plant health a 'no opinion' bars adoption, but the Commission may go to the appeal committee and adopt if that committee also delivers no opinion; (b) no adoption, only resubmission; (c) yes, advisory opinions do not bind.
• Framework: Art 291(3) TFEU, Regulation 182/2011; committees of Member State representatives chaired by the Commission; examination procedure = QMV (Art 16(4) TEU).
• (a) No opinion: as a rule the Commission may adopt (Art 5(4)), EXCEPT for taxation, financial services, protection of the health or safety of humans, animals or plants, definitive multilateral safeguard measures, where the basic act excludes it, or where a simple majority of members opposes. A pesticide concerns health → no adoption now, but referral to the appeal committee; if it too gives no opinion, the Commission may adopt (Art 6(3)) – as with glyphosate.
• (b) Negative opinion (QMV against): the Commission shall not adopt the draft; it may within two months submit an amended version to the same committee or within one month submit it to the appeal committee (Art 5(3)).
• (c) Advisory procedure (Art 4): opinion by simple majority, non-binding; the Commission decides, taking the utmost account of the committee's conclusions – it may adopt despite a negative vote.
• EP and Council may at any time indicate that a draft exceeds the implementing powers (right of scrutiny, Art 11) – not binding.
Codex: Art 291 TFEU; Art 16(4) TEU · Regulation 182/2011, Art 4, 5, 6, 11 (not in codex).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: (a) A Commission implementing regulation contradicts the basic regulation under which it was adopted. (b) A directive of 2025 contradicts an earlier regulation of 2019 on the same subject. (c) An Austrian court considers that an EU directive violates the Charter and wants to declare it invalid itself. Describe the hierarchy of norms in EU law and resolve each conflict. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Primary law > international agreements > secondary law > tertiary law > (all) national law; (a) the implementing act is unlawful, (b) lex specialis/lex posterior decide, not the type of act, (c) only the CJEU can declare an EU act invalid (Foto-Frost).
• Hierarchy: primary law (TEU, TFEU, Charter, protocols, general principles) → international agreements of the Union (Art 216(2) TFEU) → secondary law (regulations, directives, decisions, whether legislative or directly based on the Treaties) → tertiary law (delegated and implementing acts, Art 290–291 TFEU) → national law of every rank (primacy). Lower norms must be interpreted in conformity with higher ones and are invalid if they conflict.
• (a) Tertiary law must respect its basic act; the implementing regulation is unlawful – annulment within two months (Art 263 TFEU), plea of illegality (Art 277) or reference on validity (Art 267).
• (b) Regulations and directives have the same rank; conflicts are resolved by lex specialis derogat legi generali and lex posterior derogat legi priori – the later directive prevails unless the regulation is the more specific rule. (Within primary law too there is no internal hierarchy.)
• (c) National courts may find EU acts valid, but may not declare them invalid; they must refer the question to the CJEU (Art 267 TFEU; Foto-Frost, 314/85), which reviews the directive against the Charter (Art 6(1) TEU; e.g. Digital Rights Ireland, C-293/12, invalidating the Data Retention Directive – referred partly by the Austrian Constitutional Court).
Codex: Art 6 TEU; Art 216(2), 263, 267, 277, 288–291 TFEU · Foto-Frost (314/85), Digital Rights Ireland (C-293/12).

cards.q: Italy nationalised its electricity industry in 1962. Mr Costa, a shareholder of an expropriated company, refused to pay his electricity bill and argued before a Milan court that the nationalisation law infringed the EEC Treaty. The Italian Constitutional Court had held that the later Italian statute prevailed over the Treaty, which had been ratified by an ordinary statute. How did the Court of Justice decide the conflict, and how does it justify the primacy of EU law? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: In Costa v ENEL (6/64, 1964) the Court held that EU law, as an independent source of law, cannot be overridden by domestic provisions 'however framed', not even by later statutes; primacy rests on the autonomy of the legal order, the transfer of sovereignty, uniformity and effectiveness.
• Autonomy: unlike ordinary international treaties, the EEC Treaty created its own legal system which on entry into force became an integral part of the Member States' legal systems and which their courts are bound to apply (building on Van Gend en Loos, 26/62: 'new legal order').
• Transfer of sovereignty: by creating a Community of unlimited duration with its own institutions, personality, legal capacity and real powers stemming from a limitation of sovereignty or transfer of powers, the Member States have limited their sovereign rights and created a body of law binding their nationals and themselves.
• Reciprocity and uniformity: states cannot give precedence to a unilateral and subsequent measure over a legal order accepted on a basis of reciprocity; the executive force of EU law cannot vary from one state to another without jeopardising the Treaty's objectives and causing prohibited discrimination (Art 18 TFEU).
• Textual arguments: the duty of loyalty (then Art 5 EEC, now Art 4(3) TEU – not Art 3(3) TEU); direct applicability of regulations (then Art 189, now Art 288(2) TFEU) would be meaningless if states could nullify it by legislation; special derogation clauses would be superfluous.
• Result: lex posterior does not apply; the conflicting Italian statute cannot prevail. There is no express Treaty article – only Declaration 17 recalls the case law.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 18, 288(2) TFEU; Declaration 17 · Costa v ENEL (6/64), Van Gend en Loos (26/62).

cards.q: Why and to what extent is the primacy of EU law a conflict-resolution rule? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Primacy decides which of two conflicting norms applies in a concrete case (application primacy), without annulling the national norm, and only to the extent of a genuine conflict within the scope of a directly effective EU rule.
• Why: EU law and national law are two autonomous but interlocking legal orders that may claim to govern the same situation; primacy tells the national judge and administration which rule to apply, ensuring the uniform and effective application of EU law (Costa v ENEL, 6/64; Simmenthal, 106/77).
• Application, not validity: incompatibility does not render the national rule non-existent or void; the national court must disapply it in the case at hand (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97). The national rule remains valid and continues to govern situations outside the scope of EU law (e.g. purely internal situations – possible reverse discrimination).
• Extent/limits: (1) a genuine conflict is required – first try conform interpretation; (2) disapplication presupposes a directly effective EU provision, otherwise only conform interpretation or state liability remain (Popławski II, C-573/17); (3) the Member State must still repeal or amend the incompatible law for legal certainty (Commission v France, 167/73). Exception: decisions of bodies that are not independent tribunals may be treated as null and void (W.Ż., C-487/19).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 258, 288 TFEU; Declaration 17 · Costa, Simmenthal, IN.CO.GE.'90, Popławski II, Commission v France (167/73).

cards.q: Does EU law enjoy primacy over national constitutional law according to the Court of Justice? Discuss, with reference to case law, and explain how the Treaties take account of national constitutional identity. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – for the CJEU every rule of EU law prevails over every rule of national law, including constitutional provisions and fundamental rights (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70); national identity is respected only within EU law through Art 4(2) TEU, as interpreted by the CJEU.
• Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70, 1970): the validity or effect of a Union measure cannot be affected by allegations that it runs counter to fundamental rights as formulated by a national constitution or the principles of a national constitutional structure; in return the Court protects fundamental rights as general principles of EU law.
• Illustrations: Kreil (C-285/98) – the German constitutional exclusion of women from armed service yielded to the equal-treatment directive; Melloni (C-399/11) – Spain could not impose a higher national constitutional standard on European Arrest Warrant surrenders where EU law is exhaustive (Art 53 Charter).
• National identity: the Union respects the Member States' national identities inherent in their fundamental structures (Art 4(2) TEU) – but as a ground of justification within EU law, e.g. the Austrian law abolishing nobility justified a restriction of free movement (Sayn-Wittgenstein, C-208/09; see also Omega, C-36/02). It does not allow a national court to disapply EU law unilaterally (RS, C-430/21).
• Contrast: national constitutional courts (Germany, Austria, Czechia, Poland …) claim an integration-proof core and ultra vires review – that is their perspective, not the CJEU's.
Codex: Art 4(2), 6 TEU; Art 53 Charter · Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Kreil, Melloni, Sayn-Wittgenstein, RS (C-430/21).

cards.q: Simmentel AG imports beef from France into Austria and is charged veterinary inspection fees under an Austrian federal statute that clearly conflicts with a directly applicable EU regulation. The district court is convinced of the conflict but believes that, under national law, only the Austrian Constitutional Court may set aside a federal statute. (a) What must the district court do? (b) Would an Austrian customs office have to apply the statute? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) The district court must itself disapply the statute without waiting for the Constitutional Court (Simmenthal, 106/77); (b) no – administrative authorities are also bound to disapply (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88).
• Simmenthal (106/77, 1978): every national court must, in a case within its jurisdiction, apply EU law in its entirety and protect the rights it confers on individuals, and must accordingly set aside any conflicting provision of national law, whether prior or subsequent to the EU rule, if necessary of its own motion; it need not request or await the prior setting aside of the national provision by legislative or other constitutional means. Otherwise the effectiveness of directly applicable EU rules and of Art 267 TFEU would be impaired.
• (a) The national rule reserving the review of statutes to the Constitutional Court cannot prevent the district court from disapplying the statute; if in doubt about interpretation it may refer to the CJEU (Art 267(2) TFEU). A national priority procedure for constitutional review is compatible only if courts remain free to refer at any time and to disapply (Melki, C-188/10). The fees cannot be charged; Simmentel may claim repayment.
• (b) The duty to apply EU law and disapply conflicting national law binds all organs of the state, including administrative authorities and municipalities (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88), based on Art 4(3) TEU.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 267, 288(2) TFEU · Simmenthal (106/77), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88), Melki (C-188/10).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements and indicate whether they are true or false. (a) 'The primacy of EU law is expressly laid down in Art 4(3) TEU.' (b) 'A national statute that conflicts with a directly applicable EU regulation is void.' (c) 'Only courts, not administrative authorities, must disapply national law that conflicts with EU law.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false.
• (a) False. No Treaty article establishes primacy; it is judge-made (Costa v ENEL, 6/64). The Constitutional Treaty (Art I-6) would have codified it but failed; the Lisbon Treaty only annexed Declaration 17, which recalls that 'in accordance with well settled case law' the Treaties and EU law have primacy 'under the conditions laid down by the said case law', together with an opinion of the Council Legal Service. Art 4(3) TEU (sincere cooperation) is only one of the supporting arguments.
• (b) False. Primacy is application primacy, not validity primacy: the national statute is not void or non-existent but must be disapplied in the individual case (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97); it remains applicable outside the scope of EU law. The Member State must still amend it for legal certainty (Commission v France, 167/73).
• (c) False. All state organs must give full effect to EU law, including administrative authorities (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88; Art 4(3) TEU); and every court, not only the constitutional court, may and must disapply (Simmenthal, 106/77).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Declaration 17 · Costa v ENEL, IN.CO.GE.'90, Fratelli Costanzo, Simmenthal.

cards.q: To what extent is the theory of the 'integration-proof core' of national constitutions connected with the so-called Solange case law? Which court delivered the Solange decisions? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The German Federal Constitutional Court (BVerfG) delivered Solange I (1974) and Solange II (1986); they reserve protection of a core of the Basic Law – fundamental rights – against EU law, the origin of the integration-proof core doctrine.
• Integration-proof core: the part of a national constitution that EU law cannot override – in Germany the eternity clause of Art 79(3) Basic Law, applied via Art 23(1); in EU law its echo is national identity (Art 4(2) TEU).
• Solange I (1974): 'as long as' the Community lacked a fundamental-rights catalogue equivalent to the Basic Law, the BVerfG would review Community law against German fundamental rights.
• Solange II (1986): 'as long as' the Community – through the CJEU's case law (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Nold) – ensures protection substantially similar to the Basic Law, the BVerfG will not exercise that review. The reservation was suspended, not abandoned (later identity and ultra vires review).
• The CJEU never accepted it (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft); dialogue avoided a 'show-down'.
Codex: Art 4(2), 6 TEU · Solange I (BVerfGE 37, 271), Solange II (BVerfGE 73, 339), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70).

cards.q: (a) What is an ultra vires act? (b) Under which conditions does the German Federal Constitutional Court claim the right to declare an EU act ultra vires? (c) Describe the PSPP conflict and the reaction of the EU. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: An ultra vires act is an act of an EU institution or body adopted beyond the competences conferred on the Union; for the CJEU only it can declare such an act invalid, while the BVerfG claims a residual review under strict conditions (Honeywell) and used it in PSPP (2020).
• (a) EU perspective: the Union and its institutions may act only within the competences conferred (Art 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU); an act exceeding them is unlawful and can be annulled for lack of competence (Art 263(2) TFEU) or declared invalid in a preliminary ruling (Art 267) – exclusively by the CJEU (Foto-Frost, 314/85); until then it is presumed valid. National perspective: an act outside the 'integration programme' approved by the national ratification act lacks democratic legitimation and is inapplicable in that state (BVerfG Maastricht 1993, Lisbon 2009). Note: breaches of EU law by Member States are infringements, not ultra vires acts.
• (b) Honeywell (BVerfG 2010): ultra vires review only (1) after giving the CJEU the opportunity to rule via a preliminary reference, and (2) if the breach of competence is sufficiently qualified – manifest and leading to a structurally significant shift of competences to the detriment of the Member States.
• (c) PSPP: on the BVerfG's reference, the CJEU upheld the ECB's public sector purchase programme as monetary policy compatible with Art 123 and 127 TFEU (Weiss, C-493/17, 2018). The BVerfG (5 May 2020) called that judgment 'objectively arbitrary' and itself ultra vires, found the ECB decisions ultra vires for lack of a proportionality assessment and barred the Bundesbank from participating unless the ECB justified proportionality within three months. EU reaction: CJEU press release – only the CJEU can find an EU act contrary to EU law, otherwise the unity of the legal order is at risk; the Commission opened infringement proceedings against Germany (2021), closed after German commitments. The ECB supplied documents and the conflict was defused.
Codex: Art 4(2), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU; Art 123, 127, 263, 267 TFEU · Foto-Frost, Weiss (C-493/17), BVerfG Honeywell (2010) and PSPP (2 BvR 859/15).

cards.q: Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false: 'A decision of the European Commission does not have primacy over national constitutional law.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: False (from the CJEU's perspective) – primacy attaches to ANY rule of EU law, including individual Commission decisions, over ANY national law, including the constitution.
• A decision is binding in its entirety on its addressees (Art 288(4) TFEU) and is part of EU law; primacy covers primary, secondary and tertiary law alike (Costa v ENEL, 6/64) and prevails even over national constitutional rules (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70).
• Example: a Commission state-aid recovery decision must be enforced even against a final national judgment protected by res judicata (Lucchini, C-119/05). An addressee who did not challenge the decision within two months (Art 263(6) TFEU) cannot contest its validity later before national courts (TWD Textilwerke Deggendorf, C-188/92); only the CJEU can declare it invalid (Foto-Frost).
• Qualification: national constitutional courts reserve identity and ultra vires review (Solange, Honeywell, PSPP) – but that is their contested view; for the exam answer: statement false under EU law.
Codex: Art 263(6), 288(4) TFEU · Costa, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Lucchini (C-119/05), TWD (C-188/92).

cards.q: Scotland introduced a minimum retail price per unit of alcohol. On a preliminary reference the CJEU held that such a rule restricts the free movement of goods and that the national court must examine whether less restrictive measures could protect health as effectively. The first-instance court finds that there are less restrictive means. On appeal, the higher court declares that it is not bound by the CJEU judgment, overturns the decision and applies the minimum-price law without further reflection. (a) Assess the higher court's approach. (b) What can the European Commission do? (c) What can a wine importer harmed by the judgment do? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The higher court breaches EU law – a preliminary ruling binds all courts in the same proceedings; the Commission can bring infringement proceedings (Art 258 TFEU) and the importer may claim state liability for judicial breach (Köbler).
• (a) A preliminary ruling (Art 267 TFEU) binds the referring court and every national court ruling in the same case, including appellate courts; its interpretation also has de facto general effect. A court with doubts may make a new reference, but may not ignore the ruling; a court of last instance must refer if a genuine question remains (Art 267(3); CILFIT, 283/81). By applying the conflicting law 'without reflection' the court disregards the primacy of EU law (Costa, Simmenthal), Art 34–36 TFEU as interpreted, and Art 4(3) and 19(1) TEU. (In the real case, Scotch Whisky Association, C-333/14, the UK Supreme Court applied the test properly and upheld the law.)
• (b) Breaches by courts are attributable to the Member State, whose independence does not matter (Commission v Italy, C-129/00; Commission v France, C-416/17 – failure of a supreme court to refer). The Commission may open the Art 258 procedure (letter of formal notice, reasoned opinion, action); if the judgment is not complied with, Art 260(2) allows a lump sum or penalty payment imposed by the Court.
• (c) State liability for decisions of courts adjudicating at last instance (Köbler, C-224/01): the rule confers rights on individuals; the breach is sufficiently serious, i.e. the court manifestly infringed the applicable law – deliberate disregard of the CJEU's case law always is; direct causal link to the damage. National law may not exclude such liability (Traghetti del Mediterraneo, C-173/03). Action before the competent national court.
Codex: Art 4(3), 19(1) TEU; Art 34, 36, 258, 260, 267 TFEU · CILFIT, Köbler (C-224/01), Commission v France (C-416/17), Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14).

cards.q: Do all Member States accept the primacy of EU law on the same basis as the Court of Justice? Describe the position of Austria and give two examples of other national courts that have set limits to primacy. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All Member States accept primacy, but mostly on their own constitutional basis and subject to limits (integration-proof core, identity, ultra vires); Austria accepts it via the 1994 accession as a total revision of the constitution, with the leading principles as the limit.
• General: acceptance on the assumption that the Union stays within its competences; several states (Austria, Czechia, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland) reserve limits – the dispute is about who has the last word.
• Austria: accession was approved by referendum (12 June 1994) as a total revision of the Federal Constitution (Art 44(3) B-VG), so EU law takes precedence even over ordinary constitutional law. Prevailing view: limit = the leading principles ('Baugesetze') of the B-VG – democratic, republican, federal and rule-of-law principles; an EU development violating them would require a new total revision with referendum. The Constitutional Court (VfGH) treats Charter rights as constitutionally guaranteed rights in its review (U 466/11, 2012) and makes preliminary references.
• Germany: BVerfG – Solange, identity review (Lisbon 2009) and ultra vires review (Honeywell 2010, PSPP 2020).
• Czech Republic: the Constitutional Court declared the CJEU's Landtová judgment (C-399/09) ultra vires in the Slovak Pensions case (Pl. ÚS 5/12, 2012) – the first such finding.
• Poland: the Constitutional Tribunal (K 3/21, 2021) declared Treaty provisions as interpreted by the CJEU incompatible with the Polish Constitution; the Commission brought infringement proceedings. (Also: Danish Supreme Court, Ajos 2016.)
Codex: Art 4(2) TEU; Declaration 17 · Landtová (C-399/09); national decisions are not in the codex.

cards.q: The Constitutional Court of Member State Dacia rules that a CJEU judgment requiring national courts to disapply limitation periods in corruption cases violates Dacian constitutional identity, and that ordinary courts must not follow it. Judge Popescu nevertheless applies the CJEU judgment and faces disciplinary proceedings. (a) Is the Constitutional Court entitled to rely on Art 4(2) TEU in this way? (b) What must Judge Popescu do? (c) What can the EU do? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – national identity cannot justify a unilateral refusal to apply EU law as interpreted by the CJEU; the judge must disapply the Constitutional Court's ruling and may not be disciplined for applying EU law (RS, C-430/21).
• (a) Art 4(2) TEU obliges the Union to respect national identity, but its scope is determined within EU law by the CJEU; a national constitutional court may not declare a CJEU interpretation inapplicable on identity grounds – if it has concerns it must make a preliminary reference (Art 267 TFEU). Otherwise primacy, equality of Member States before the Treaties and the uniform application of EU law would collapse (RS, C-430/21, 2022; Euro Box Promotion, C-357/19).
• (b) Under primacy and Simmenthal (106/77) she must apply EU law and set aside the conflicting national case law, even of a constitutional court; a lower court is not bound by instructions of a higher court that are contrary to EU law (Elchinov, C-173/09) and may refer to the CJEU at any time. Disciplinary liability of judges for applying EU law or making a reference infringes judicial independence (Art 19(1) second subpara TEU; Art 47 Charter).
• (c) The Commission may bring an infringement action (Art 258 TFEU) – acts of all state organs, including constitutional courts, are attributable to the state; penalties under Art 260(2); systemic threats to the rule of law may also lead to the Art 7 TEU procedure or measures under the Conditionality Regulation 2020/2092.
Codex: Art 4(2)–(3), 7, 19(1) TEU; Art 258, 260, 267 TFEU; Art 47 Charter · RS (C-430/21), Euro Box (C-357/19), Simmenthal, Elchinov (C-173/09).
